items.title: Maybe the Future Will Only Have the Liberal Arts and Engineering: Thoughts on a 3Blue1Brown Video
items.content_text: AI translation notice: This English version was translated from the original Chinese article with AI assistance. Some nuances may differ from the original. Tonight I watched 3Blue1Brown's video “There Has Never Been a Better Time to Devote Yourself to Mathematics,” and it stirred up some feelings. I will record them briefly here. I have put the link below so everyone can watch it directly. After finishing the whole video, I want to start with an attention-grabbing hot take: if we really do reach the point 3Blue1Brown describes, where AI is stronger than humans at everything humans do, then from that point on all learning will become liberal arts. Fun fact: in English, both the arts and the liberal arts are called Art. So when people in China say they are studying the liberal arts, they could equally say they are studying art. Which means that in the future, mathematics could become a so-called “liberal art” as well. Push that condition a little further, and all research—physics, chemistry, even every other kind of theoretical work—could become a liberal art. In the future there will be no distinction between the liberal arts and the sciences, only between “arts” and “engineering”. One is learning theory; the other is landing theory in practice and interacting with the real world. At that point, university will no longer be a stage of educational attainment, but a higher-order club—one where the entrance ticket is an assessment you have to pass. Everyone inside is passionate about learning, wants to learn, and likes discussing with people who share that passion, to socialize and to connect. The reason people join this club in the first place is that they were infected by people who carry that kind of passion—just as my original motivation for building this blog site came from being inspired by many like-minded people online who actually put their ideas into practice. University would then no longer be simply a few years you have to put aside in order to land a better job. This seems to loop back to how aristocrats studied science in the seventeenth and eighteenth centuries. Under the development of AGI, productivity advances, and with it comes a reasonable new mode of distribution. Because the means of production would no longer be owned by fixed capital; they would be generated by AGI. The relations of production would change as well, and distribution would necessarily change with them. Given a good distribution mechanism, people would no longer worry about making a living, and could pursue the things they love. Those who love painting would paint, those who love sports would play sports, or those who love studying mathematical theory would study it, turn theory into practice, or even just spread the joy of learning and rope more people in, or simply teach it to children. In the end, all of it becomes a kind of “service industry,” or a way of life that people enjoy. At that point, doing research would be like what The Craftsman describes: the reason for doing something well is simply that you want to get it done, and so you do it well. The inner impulse to “do a job well for its own sake.” Of course I know this is idealistic, but it really does sound lovely, doesn't it? With AGI developing continuously, perhaps the whole industry, the whole society, has realized that it is going to have to change. Look at current policy: many graduate students no longer need to write a thesis, and instead have this “Outstanding Engineer” training mechanism. All of these are changes produced in order to adapt to social development. In my view, when it comes to social development, holding fast to the unchanging in order to meet every change rarely works; against the patterns of history, it has almost never happened. We are going to change in any case, and only by changing constantly can we use new ideas to solve new problems. If we do not know what it will turn into, why not imagine it as something a little better? —Written on a night tormented by linear algebra transcribed from speech

The reason people join this club in the first place is that they were infected by people who carry that kind of passion—just as my original motivation for building this blog site came from being inspired by many like-minded people online who actually put their ideas into practice. University would then no longer be simply a few years you have to put aside in order to land a better job.

This seems to loop back to how aristocrats studied science in the seventeenth and eighteenth centuries. Under the development of AGI, productivity advances, and with it comes a reasonable new mode of distribution. Because the means of production would no longer be owned by fixed capital; they would be generated by AGI. The relations of production would change as well, and distribution would necessarily change with them.

Given a good distribution mechanism, people would no longer worry about making a living, and could pursue the things they love. Those who love painting would paint, those who love sports would play sports, or those who love studying mathematical theory would study it, turn theory into practice, or even just spread the joy of learning and rope more people in, or simply teach it to children.

In the end, all of it becomes a kind of “service industry,” or a way of life that people enjoy.

At that point, doing research would be like what The Craftsman describes: the reason for doing something well is simply that you want to get it done, and so you do it well.

The inner impulse to “do a job well for its own sake.”

Of course I know this is idealistic, but it really does sound lovely, doesn't it?

With AGI developing continuously, perhaps the whole industry, the whole society, has realized that it is going to have to change. Look at current policy: many graduate students no longer need to write a thesis, and instead have this “Outstanding Engineer” training mechanism. In my view, when it comes to social development, holding fast to the unchanging in order to meet every change rarely works; against the patterns of history, it has almost never happened. We are going to change in any case, and only by changing constantly can we use new ideas to solve new problems.

If we do not know what it will turn into, why not imagine it as something a little better?

items.title: From the 408 OS Exam to Production: Why Is the Signal-Sending Function Called kill Instead of send?
items.content_text: AI translation notice: This English version was translated from the original Chinese article with AI assistance. Some nuances may differ from the original. Recently, while reviewing the “Process” chapter of the 408 operating systems course, I got to the signal mechanism of inter-process communication IPC . Since this round was the intensive review phase, I was reading the textbook very carefully. I froze for a moment: “Wait—sending a signal between processes, and the system call is called kill ?” That cannot be right. Is all inter-process communication meant to kill the other party? To use an analogy: you send a friend a message saying “come downstairs and hang out,” and someone calls that operation . That is absurd, and genuinely counterintuitive, so I dug in a little deeper to find out what was going on. Why did the UNIX forefathers choose such a misleading name? Today let us dig into this “legacy naming” that has stayed with us for decades, and take a look at what it actually means in everyday development and in interviews. The “Force Kill” the Name Misleads You Into When I first saw the system call, or the command in a terminal, I formed an obvious assumption: its only job is to “take out a process.” When troubleshooting a production incident or debugging a program, we habitually type , or the more brutal , into a terminal. As the process vanishes instantly, I naturally equated that operation with the way a program ends. But in fact, that intuition of mine concealed a major technical misunderstanding. The essence of is to deliver a signal to a specified process , not to “kill” it in the literal sense. Terminating the process is merely the default behavior of a process on receiving a particular signal, not a functional limit of the system call itself. In other words, is nothing more than an asynchronous communication mechanism for notifications, and “killing” is just one default result among many ways of handling signals. What Does Actually Do? Let us first look at how is normally used. In C, the prototype of the system call is very simple: : the ID card number of the target process. : the number of the signal you want to send such as , , and so on . If you pass for known as the null signal , does not send a signal at all; it is used to probe whether the process exists and whether the current user has permission to send it signals commonly used for liveness checks when writing daemons . A Simple C Example The code below shows how to send a custom signal to a specified process, and how to check the process's status: Here, merely delivers the signal into the kernel's process control block PCB , completing a lightweight event notification. The Historical Puzzle: Why and Not ? Since its essence is sending a signal, why is it not called , or simply ? That would seem more intuitive. Answering that means rewinding to the wild early days of UNIX in the 1970s. Historical constraints and original intent : In the earliest UNIX designs, inter-process communication was nowhere near as complex as it is today. There were very few kinds of signals, and the one purpose, the core scenario, they were designed for was— terminating processes that had run out of control, were stuck in an infinite loop, or were hogging resources . So the intuitive mission of this system call at the time was “take it out,” and the name was extremely apt. Path dependence in the POSIX standard : As systems evolved, people found this “asynchronous notification mechanism” too useful to confine to killing processes; it could also announce state changes, reload configuration, report that a child process had exited, and more. Signals multiplied, and the feature expanded into general-purpose IPC. But by then the name had already taken root in countless system source files and early books. To maintain backward compatibility, the POSIX standard ultimately kept the name. Distinction from data-transfer APIs : Names like and usually accompany the transfer of large byte streams in network programming and pipes. Traditional UNIX signals, by contrast, are extremely lightweight: they carry no extra data payload modern can pass a small amount of data, but that is an extension , and convey only a pure event notification that “something happened.” So avoiding also avoids confusion with data transfer. Common Signals at a Glance During development and in interviews, a handful of high-frequency signals are worth knowing. Here I had AI summarize them for me, which also makes them handy for later use: Signal Name Default Number Default Behavior Typical Use Case / Meaning --- --- --- --- SIGHUP 1 Terminates the process Sent when the terminal disconnects; modern servers often repurpose it as Nginx/daemon “reload configuration” SIGINT 2 Terminates the process Ctrl + C , interrupts the foreground process SIGQUIT 3 Core dump and terminate Ctrl + \\ backslash , which not only quits but leaves a core dump file for debugging SIGKILL 9 Forcibly kills the process Cannot be caught or ignored . The kernel reclaims it directly; the program does not even get a chance to say goodbye SIGSEGV 11 Core dump and terminate Segmentation fault illegal memory access, such as a wild pointer or out-of-bounds access SIGPIPE 13 Terminates the process Triggered by continuing to write to a pipe/socket with no read end SIGALRM 14 Terminates the process Timer expiration triggered by the function SIGTERM 15 Terminates the process Software termination what the default command sends . Can be caught , and is the first choice for graceful shutdown SIGSTOP 19 Suspends the process Cannot be caught or ignored . Suspends execution like pressing pause SIGCONT 18 Resumes the process Resumes a process suspended by or for some other reason SIGUSR1/2 30/31 Terminates the process User-defined signals; developers can assign them whatever business meaning they like AI also went ahead and wrote an extra exam question all on its own, so I will record it here too: 💡 A high-frequency interview question : Why can 9 and 19 not be caught or ignored? Answer : Because they are the kernel's “absolute control” reserved for the administrator. If user code were allowed to catch , and someone happened to write an infinite loop that catches it and does nothing, the system could never again kill that rogue process by conventional means, and the whole system would spin completely out of control. Real-World Use Cases Where does the command actually get used day to day? Again, I had AI give me a quick summary: Daily Operations in the Shell : sends SIGTERM 15 by default. It gives the process a polite hint: “Buddy, that is about enough—wrap up what you are doing and head out.” : sends SIGKILL 9 . “No more talk—vanish this instant!” Note: using all the time easily leads to disasters such as uncommitted database transactions, temp files left behind, and unreleased locks. : sends SIGHUP 1 . In servers such as Nginx, it is commonly used for hot reloading: on receiving it, the master process reloads its configuration and gracefully restarts the worker processes, with zero service interruption. Backend Development and Graceful Shutdown When writing web services in Go, Java, or Node.js, if we stop a container with Docker which sends or press in a terminal which sends , the program cannot simply drop dead. A competent backend framework will listen for these termination signals : After receiving , stop accepting new HTTP requests. Finish the requests currently in flight and write them to the database. Disconnect from Redis and MySQL, release resources safely, and then exit gracefully. Simple Inter-Process Communication IPC In some multi-process daemons such as the Master-Worker pattern , the master process can use to tell a child process: “The log file has been rotated, so please reopen the log file handle.” What Should Ordinary Developers Watch Out For? Even if you usually write high-level business code and never call the system-level directly, you have definitely hit—or will sooner or later hit—the following signal-related “reefs”: The power of Ctrl+C : You run a long script in a terminal, your hand slips, and you press . In essence, the terminal driver has just sent to the foreground process group. Zombie processes and : A parent process forks a child; if the child dies and the parent never reaps its status through , the child becomes a zombie process. And when the child exits, the kernel sends the parent a signal. Many high-performance frameworks reap child processes efficiently precisely by catching asynchronously. Interrupted system calls : If your program is in the middle of a blocking I/O operation such as a on a socket , and a signal arrives and its handler runs, that may be interrupted and return , with set to . When writing low-level network libraries, you must explicitly handle this “interrupted by a signal” case usually by wrapping it in an outer loop and retrying . Async-signal safety Async-Signal-Safe : When writing a signal handler, what you can do inside it is extremely limited. Never call non-thread-safe or non-async-signal-safe functions such as or inside a signal handler, or you may easily cause deadlocks or memory corruption that are very hard to track down. Signals do not queue non-real-time signals get lost : Traditional standard signals 1–31 do not queue. If the same signal is sent to a process several times in quick succession, the process may only perceive it once. If your business logic absolutely cannot drop a single event, standard signals will not do the job you need real-time signals, or RT signals . Conclusion After going through all of this, I finally truly digested the inter-process communication function, and a little extra reading also gave me a deeper understanding of IPC. But honestly, this kind of misunderstanding is scary. Without AI helping me summarize things and answer my questions, I probably would not have wanted to research on my own why the IPC function is called for quite a while; I might have just assumed that inter-process communication exists entirely to finish the other party off. I also wonder how much more historical debt like this is out there... I hope this note can also help developers who are grinding through 408 operating systems, or whose scalps are tingling from wrestling with Linux signals, finally sort out the technical truth behind this historical baggage.
items.content_html:
AI translation notice: This English version was translated from the original Chinese article with AI assistance. Some nuances may differ from the original.

Recently, while reviewing the “Process” chapter of the 408 operating systems course, I got to the signal mechanism of inter-process communication (IPC). Since this round was the intensive review phase, I was reading the textbook very carefully.

I froze for a moment: “Wait—sending a signal between processes, and the system call is called kill()?”

That cannot be right. Is all inter-process communication meant to kill the other party? To use an analogy: you send a friend a message saying “come downstairs and hang out,” and someone calls that operation execute_friend(best_buddy). That is absurd, and genuinely counterintuitive, so I dug in a little deeper to find out what was going on.

Why did the UNIX forefathers choose such a misleading name? Today let us dig into this “legacy naming” that has stayed with us for decades, and take a look at what it actually means in everyday development and in interviews.

The “Force Kill” the Name Misleads You Into

When I first saw the kill() system call, or the kill command in a terminal, I formed an obvious assumption: its only job is to “take out a process.”

When troubleshooting a production incident or debugging a program, we habitually type kill <pid>, or the more brutal kill -9 <pid>, into a terminal. As the process vanishes instantly, I naturally equated that operation with the way a program ends.

But in fact, that intuition of mine concealed a major technical misunderstanding.

The essence of kill() is to deliver a signal to a specified process, not to “kill” it in the literal sense. Terminating the process is merely the default behavior of a process on receiving a particular signal, not a functional limit of the system call itself. In other words, kill is nothing more than an asynchronous communication mechanism for notifications, and “killing” is just one default result among many ways of handling signals.

What Does kill(pid, sig) Actually Do?

Let us first look at how kill() is normally used.

In C, the prototype of the kill() system call is very simple:

#include <sys/types.h>
#include <signal.h>

int kill(pid_t pid, int sig);
  • pid: the ID card number of the target process.
  • sig: the number of the signal you want to send (such as SIGTERM, SIGUSR1, and so on). If you pass 0 for sig (known as the null signal), kill() does not send a signal at all; it is used to probe whether the process exists and whether the current user has permission to send it signals (commonly used for liveness checks when writing daemons).

A Simple C Example

The code below shows how to send a custom signal (SIGUSR1) to a specified process, and how to check the process's status:

#include <stdio.h>
#include <stdlib.h>
#include <sys/types.h>
#include <signal.h>
#include <unistd.h>

int main(int argc, char *argv[]){
    if (argc != 2) {
        fprintf(stderr, "Usage: %s <pid>\n", argv[0]);
        exit(1);
    }

    pid_t target_pid = atoi(argv[1]);

    // 1. 探测进程是否存在
    if (kill(target_pid, 0) == 0) {
        printf("进程 %d 存活，正在发送自定义信号 SIGUSR1...\n", target_pid);
        // 2. 发送 SIGUSR1 信号
        kill(target_pid, SIGUSR1);
    } else {
        perror("进程不存在或无权限");
    }

    return 0;
}

Here, kill() merely delivers the signal into the kernel's process control block (PCB), completing a lightweight event notification.

The Historical Puzzle: Why kill and Not send?

Since its essence is sending a signal, why is it not called send_signal(), or simply send()? That would seem more intuitive.

Answering that means rewinding to the wild early days of UNIX in the 1970s.

  1. Historical constraints and original intent: In the earliest UNIX designs, inter-process communication was nowhere near as complex as it is today. There were very few kinds of signals, and the one purpose, the core scenario, they were designed for was—terminating processes that had run out of control, were stuck in an infinite loop, or were hogging resources. So the intuitive mission of this system call at the time was “take it out,” and the name kill was extremely apt.
  2. Path dependence in the POSIX standard: As systems evolved, people found this “asynchronous notification mechanism” too useful to confine to killing processes; it could also announce state changes, reload configuration, report that a child process had exited, and more. Signals multiplied, and the feature expanded into general-purpose IPC. But by then the name kill() had already taken root in countless system source files and early books. To maintain backward compatibility, the POSIX standard ultimately kept the name.
  3. Distinction from data-transfer APIs: Names like send() and sendto() usually accompany the transfer of large byte streams in network programming and pipes. Traditional UNIX signals, by contrast, are extremely lightweight: they carry no extra data payload (modern sigqueue can pass a small amount of data, but that is an extension), and convey only a pure event notification that “something happened.” So avoiding send also avoids confusion with data transfer.

Common Signals at a Glance

During development and in interviews, a handful of high-frequency signals are worth knowing. Here I had AI summarize them for me, which also makes them handy for later use:

Signal Name Default Number Default Behavior Typical Use Case / Meaning
SIGHUP 1 Terminates the process Sent when the terminal disconnects; modern servers often repurpose it as Nginx/daemon “reload configuration”
SIGINT 2 Terminates the process Ctrl + C, interrupts the foreground process
SIGQUIT 3 Core dump and terminate Ctrl + \ (backslash), which not only quits but leaves a core dump file for debugging
SIGKILL 9 Forcibly kills the process Cannot be caught or ignored. The kernel reclaims it directly; the program does not even get a chance to say goodbye
SIGSEGV 11 Core dump and terminate Segmentation fault (illegal memory access, such as a wild pointer or out-of-bounds access)
SIGPIPE 13 Terminates the process Triggered by continuing to write to a pipe/socket with no read end
SIGALRM 14 Terminates the process Timer expiration (triggered by the alarm() function)
SIGTERM 15 Terminates the process Software termination (what the default kill command sends). Can be caught, and is the first choice for graceful shutdown
SIGSTOP 19 Suspends the process Cannot be caught or ignored. Suspends execution (like pressing pause)
SIGCONT 18 Resumes the process Resumes a process suspended by SIGSTOP or for some other reason
SIGUSR1/2 30/31 Terminates the process User-defined signals; developers can assign them whatever business meaning they like

AI also went ahead and wrote an extra exam question all on its own, so I will record it here too:

💡 A high-frequency interview question:

Why can SIGKILL (9) and SIGSTOP (19) not be caught or ignored?

Answer: Because they are the kernel's “absolute control” reserved for the administrator. If user code were allowed to catch SIGKILL, and someone happened to write an infinite loop that catches it and does nothing, the system could never again kill that rogue process by conventional means, and the whole system would spin completely out of control.

Real-World Use Cases

Where does the kill command actually get used day to day? Again, I had AI give me a quick summary:

1. Daily Operations in the Shell

  • kill <pid>: sends SIGTERM (15) by default. It gives the process a polite hint: “Buddy, that is about enough—wrap up what you are doing and head out.”
  • kill -9 <pid>: sends SIGKILL (9). “No more talk—vanish this instant!” (Note: using 9 all the time easily leads to disasters such as uncommitted database transactions, temp files left behind, and unreleased locks.)
  • kill -HUP <pid>: sends SIGHUP (1). In servers such as Nginx, it is commonly used for hot reloading: on receiving it, the master process reloads its configuration and gracefully restarts the worker processes, with zero service interruption.

2. Backend Development and Graceful Shutdown

When writing web services in Go, Java, or Node.js, if we stop a container with Docker (which sends SIGTERM) or press Ctrl+C in a terminal (which sends SIGINT), the program cannot simply drop dead.
A competent backend framework will listen for these termination signals:

  • After receiving SIGTERM, stop accepting new HTTP requests.
  • Finish the requests currently in flight and write them to the database.
  • Disconnect from Redis and MySQL, release resources safely, and then exit gracefully.

3. Simple Inter-Process Communication (IPC)

In some multi-process daemons (such as the Master-Worker pattern), the master process can use kill(worker_pid, SIGUSR1) to tell a child process: “The log file has been rotated, so please reopen the log file handle.”

What Should Ordinary Developers Watch Out For?

Even if you usually write high-level business code and never call the system-level kill() directly, you have definitely hit—or will sooner or later hit—the following signal-related “reefs”:

  1. The power of Ctrl+C: You run a long script in a terminal, your hand slips, and you press Ctrl+C. In essence, the terminal driver has just sent SIGINT to the foreground process group.
  2. Zombie processes and SIGCHLD: A parent process forks a child; if the child dies and the parent never reaps its status through wait(), the child becomes a zombie process. And when the child exits, the kernel sends the parent a SIGCHLD signal. Many high-performance frameworks reap child processes efficiently precisely by catching SIGCHLD asynchronously.
  3. Interrupted system calls (EINTR): If your program is in the middle of a blocking I/O operation (such as a read on a socket), and a signal arrives and its handler runs, that read may be interrupted and return 1, with errno set to EINTR. When writing low-level network libraries, you must explicitly handle this “interrupted by a signal” case (usually by wrapping it in an outer while loop and retrying).
  4. Async-signal safety (Async-Signal-Safe): When writing a signal handler, what you can do inside it is extremely limited. Never call non-thread-safe or non-async-signal-safe functions such as printf() or malloc() inside a signal handler, or you may easily cause deadlocks or memory corruption that are very hard to track down.
  5. Signals do not queue (non-real-time signals get lost): Traditional standard signals (1–31) do not queue. If the same signal is sent to a process several times in quick succession, the process may only perceive it once. If your business logic absolutely cannot drop a single event, standard signals will not do the job (you need real-time signals, or RT signals).

Conclusion

After going through all of this, I finally truly digested the inter-process communication function, and a little extra reading also gave me a deeper understanding of IPC.

But honestly, this kind of misunderstanding is scary. Without AI helping me summarize things and answer my questions, I probably would not have wanted to research on my own why the IPC function is called kill() for quite a while; I might have just assumed that inter-process communication exists entirely to finish the other party off. I also wonder how much more historical debt like this is out there...

I hope this note can also help developers who are grinding through 408 operating systems, or whose scalps are tingling from wrestling with Linux signals, finally sort out the technical truth behind this historical baggage.

items.title: Why Do Some Websites Have “www” and Others Don’t? — The Modern Configuration Edition
items.content_text: AI translation notice: This English version was translated from the original Chinese article with AI assistance. Some nuances may differ from the original. Cover image: Tim Berners-Lee at the 20th anniversary celebration of the World Wide Web in 2009, reunited at CERN with the historic NeXT computer he had used to develop and run the world’s first web server, multimedia browser, and web page editor. Image credit: CERN The previous post covered where came from — a naming convention suggested by Tim Berners-Lee, and a necessary way of telling services apart in the early days. But today, now that the Web has gone from “one machine running one service” to “one IP hosting countless websites,” why is no longer a necessity? And how should we deal with those headache-inducing DNS details when deploying a site? That is what I want to cover in this post. Why Did So Many Websites Stop Using Later? Because the way the internet gets used changed. When a website still meant one machine serving one service, was useful: it kept the web service separate from the mail service and made things easier to manage. Later, as machines grew more powerful, management also became simpler and easier to maintain. In particular, virtual hosting, the HTTP request header RFC 9110 , reverse proxies, CDNs, and cloud platforms gradually became commonplace, so a single IP address could route requests to different websites based on the domain name. The domain name itself no longer had to do the job of explaining what the machine was for. This also matches the thought Tim arrived at by the end of his answer to Why www?. At the same time, is four characters shorter than . That means it is shorter everywhere it shows up — on posters, business cards, video voiceovers, billboards, and anywhere users type it in by hand. That is obviously better for promoting your own brand and getting people to notice it at a glance, so more and more websites choose the bare domain — , with no subdomain — as the address they present to the world. That does not mean is technically outdated. Keeping has some practical benefits. It tells the network infrastructure plainly that this is a website; and if you later want to split off , , or other services, the boundaries stay clearer. Cookie scope RFC 6265 can also be controlled more carefully: a site sitting on will not, by default, send host-level cookies that belong only to the site over to . Where It Actually Gets Tricky: Bare Domains and CNAME At this point you might think that since is just a subdomain, you can simply skip it. But things get a little more complicated when you deploy a website, especially the first time you try a CDN, a hosting platform, or a cloud provider. Here is a first way to understand the two most common DNS records: An A record points a name straight at an IP address. A CNAME RFC 1034 §3.6.2, RFC 1035 instead says: for this name, keep looking under another name. CNAMEs are a good fit for connecting to a hosting platform. When the platform changes its server IP, you do not need to edit your own DNS every day; you just keep pointing at the domain the platform provides. But under the traditional DNS model, once a name has a CNAME, it cannot also have records of other types — RFC 2181 §10.1 states this explicitly. The problem is that the bare domain is not an ordinary subdomain. That name itself has to carry the domain’s foundational records, such as NS and SOA; it often also holds MX records for email and TXT records for domain verification. Under the traditional rules, a bare domain cannot simply become a CNAME, because those records would then have nowhere to coexist. This is also why, in the past, many hosting platforms told you: point at a CNAME, and have the bare domain do a redirect. As an ordinary subdomain, can point at the platform quite naturally; the bare domain, because of the historical structure of DNS, is not that straightforward to handle. How Do Modern DNS Providers Solve This? Later, DNS providers offered solutions under various names, such as ALIAS, ANAME, or CNAME flattening. Their specific implementations are not entirely the same, but the idea is close: you write a CNAME-like target in the dashboard, the provider resolves that target to an IP for you, and then returns it to the resolver in a form the bare domain can use. Examples include Cloudflare CNAME Flattening, DNSimple ANAME, and AWS Route 53 Alias. The IETF once had a draft, but it has not yet become a formal standard. The provider does the extra resolution work at the DNS edge. AI translation notice: This English version was translated from the original Chinese article with AI assistance. Some nuances may differ from the original.

Cover image: Tim Berners-Lee at the 20th anniversary celebration of the World Wide Web in 2009, reunited at CERN with the historic NeXT computer he had used to develop and run the world’s first web server, multimedia browser, and web page editor. Image credit: CERN

The previous post covered where www came from — a naming convention suggested by Tim Berners-Lee, and a necessary way of telling services apart in the early days.

But today, now that the Web has gone from “one machine running one service” to “one IP hosting countless websites,” why is www no longer a necessity? And how should we deal with those headache-inducing DNS details when deploying a site? That is what I want to cover in this post.

Why Did So Many Websites Stop Using www Later?

Because the way the internet gets used changed.

When a website still meant one machine serving one service, www was useful: it kept the web service separate from the mail service and made things easier to manage.

Later, as machines grew more powerful, management also became simpler and easier to maintain. In particular, virtual hosting, the HTTP Host request header (RFC 9110), reverse proxies, CDNs, and cloud platforms gradually became commonplace, so a single IP address could route requests to different websites based on the domain name. The domain name itself no longer had to do the job of explaining what the machine was for.

This also matches the thought Tim arrived at by the end of his answer to Why www?.

At the same time, blahblah.com is four characters shorter than www.blahblah.com. That means it is shorter everywhere it shows up — on posters, business cards, video voiceovers, billboards, and anywhere users type it in by hand. That is obviously better for promoting your own brand and getting people to notice it at a glance, so more and more websites choose the bare domain — blahblah.com, with no subdomain — as the address they present to the world.

That does not mean www is technically outdated.

Keeping www has some practical benefits. It tells the network infrastructure plainly that this is a website; and if you later want to split off api.blahblah.com, static.blahblah.com, or other services, the boundaries stay clearer. Cookie scope (RFC 6265) can also be controlled more carefully: a site sitting on www.blahblah.com will not, by default, send host-level cookies that belong only to the site over to api.blahblah.com.

Where It Actually Gets Tricky: Bare Domains and CNAME

At this point you might think that since www is just a subdomain, you can simply skip it. But things get a little more complicated when you deploy a website, especially the first time you try a CDN, a hosting platform, or a cloud provider.

Here is a first way to understand the two most common DNS records:

A     blahblah.com       -> 203.0.113.10
CNAME www.blahblah.com   -> my-site.hosting-provider.com

An A record points a name straight at an IP address. A CNAME (RFC 1034 §3.6.2, RFC 1035) instead says: for this name, keep looking under another name.

CNAMEs are a good fit for connecting to a hosting platform. When the platform changes its server IP, you do not need to edit your own DNS every day; you just keep pointing at the domain the platform provides. But under the traditional DNS model, once a name has a CNAME, it cannot also have records of other types — RFC 2181 §10.1 states this explicitly.

The problem is that the bare domain blahblah.com is not an ordinary subdomain. That name itself has to carry the domain’s foundational records, such as NS and SOA; it often also holds MX records for email and TXT records for domain verification. Under the traditional rules, a bare domain cannot simply become a CNAME, because those records would then have nowhere to coexist.

This is also why, in the past, many hosting platforms told you: point www.blahblah.com at a CNAME, and have the bare domain do a redirect. As an ordinary subdomain, www can point at the platform quite naturally; the bare domain, because of the historical structure of DNS, is not that straightforward to handle.

How Do Modern DNS Providers Solve This?

Later, DNS providers offered solutions under various names, such as ALIAS, ANAME, or CNAME flattening. Their specific implementations are not entirely the same, but the idea is close: you write a CNAME-like target in the dashboard, the provider resolves that target to an IP for you, and then returns it to the resolver in a form the bare domain can use. Examples include Cloudflare CNAME Flattening, DNSimple ANAME, and AWS Route 53 Alias. The IETF once had a draft-ietf-dnsop-aname draft, but it has not yet become a formal standard.

The provider does the extra resolution work at the DNS edge. As these features became widespread, connecting a bare domain to a CDN or hosting platform was no longer as awkward as before, so “no www” became easy again.

So Which One Should I Choose?

If it is just a personal blog or a small project, you can simply go with each platform’s recommendation — and besides, there is AI now.

If you like shorter addresses, use the bare domain; if you want to keep the traditional habit, or might later separate the site from other subdomain services more clearly, use www. Both approaches can be done well, and neither is much trouble.

Whichever one you choose as the main address, you still have to get redirects and certificates right for the other. DNS has to resolve, the HTTPS certificate has to cover it, and then a 301 has to unify the redirect. Take my own site as an example — I have both configured. Feel free to click and try.

  • www.markxu.icu
  • markxu.icu

Google Search Central recommends choosing one canonical address and using a 301 redirect, so that link sharing, caching, analytics, and search engine indexing all stay consistent more easily.

Then Why Does Adding www Sometimes Fail to Load?

If a website’s bare domain loads, but manually adding www throws an error, that is uncommon, but it does happen. The reason is usually that the administrator configured only one of the addresses mentioned above.

A complete visit roughly passes through these places in order:

Browser
  -> DNS: does www.example.com have a record?
  -> Server: do I accept www.blahblah.com?
  -> HTTPS: does the certificate cover www.blahblah.com?
  -> Web app: return the page, or redirect to the canonical address

If any one of these steps is not configured properly, something goes wrong.

The simplest case is that DNS has no www record at all. The lookup result is NXDOMAIN, and the browser cannot even find the server.

It is also possible that DNS already points www.blahblah.com at the correct IP, but Nginx, Apache, or the hosting platform has no configuration for that Host, so the server returns a default page, a 404, or simply refuses the request.

There is also an ordering problem that often gets overlooked: if the user visits https://www.blahblah.com, the TLS certificate check happens before the HTTP redirect (RFC 9110 §4.2.2). If the certificate only covers blahblah.com, the browser will block the request at the HTTPS step, before the server has a chance to tell it “please go to the address without www.” That is why certificates usually need to cover both names, or you use a wildcard certificate that includes them both.

A fully configured website often lets both addresses find it, and then picks one as the canonical address:

https://www.blahblah.com  -> 301 -> https://blahblah.com
https://blahblah.com       -> 200

Of course, you can also do the reverse and redirect the bare domain to www; that is entirely your personal choice, and technically the difference is not obvious.

References

  • RFC 1034: Domain Names - Concepts and Facilities
  • RFC 1035: Domain Names - Implementation and Specification
  • RFC 2181: Clarifications to the DNS Specification §10.1
  • RFC 6265: HTTP State Management Mechanism
  • RFC 9110: HTTP Semantics
  • Cloudflare: DNS CNAME record
  • Cloudflare: CNAME Flattening
  • Google Search Central: Consolidate duplicate URLs

AI translation notice: This English version was translated from the original Chinese article with AI assistance. Some nuances may differ from the original.

The cover image is a photograph of the world's first web server: the NeXT computer that Tim Berners-Lee used at CERN.

www, meaning the World Wide Web, is a pretty basic concept — even high school teachers have already covered it.

But today, while reading a few blog sites, I suddenly noticed something I had never seriously thought about before: some URLs are www.blahblah.com, while others are just blahblah.com.

Before I looked into it, I assumed every website had a www, and that the browser simply decided those few letters could be left off, so it hid them from us. Today I got curious and did some digging, and it turns out the browser hiding is not the whole story at all. Current technology made www unnecessary a long time ago, and most modern websites have stopped using it too — where it survives, it is mostly a leftover historical habit.

So this post is mainly about the origin of the www prefix; a later one will cover why it disappeared afterward, and how we use domain names today.

First, the technical side: why does www exist at all?

The earliest Internet differed from today's Internet in plenty of infrastructure-level ways, so many of the protocols and features from back then were designed with very different intentions. If we are curious about why www exists, we probably need to start from the very beginning of the Internet.

The Early Internet — 1969

When the earliest Internet — or rather its predecessor, ARPANET (1969) — came into being, it connected the computers of a few universities and research institutes. Each machine had a hostname, registered directly in the centrally maintained HOSTS.TXT (which DNS would later replace).

The intention back then was simple: connect a few machines so they could talk to each other.

Because there were so few machines, the concept of a domain name did not exist yet, and there was no need for an extra layer of indirection. A simple “machine name → address” mapping was enough.

For the specifics of this period, see this article, Internet History Ramblings, Part 7 — ARPANET (the other posts in that series have nothing to do with this one, but they are genuinely fun — I highly recommend reading more of them)

The Arrival of DNS (Domain Names) — 1983

As more and more machines joined, the network had already become something entirely different from what it once was.

On January 1, 1983, every networked host switched from NCP to TCP/IP, an event also known as TCP/IP Flag Day.

All machines dropped support for the old protocol and supported TCP/IP instead, turning the previous “single network, flat, centralized” architecture into a “multi-network, layered, delegable” one. That also met the demand of a growing number of machines joining the network.

As more and more machines joined, the HOSTS.TXT file, previously maintained by hand at a central location, began to balloon. Back when storage was not the cheap, bottomless resource it is today, having every machine store a copy of HOST.TXT became increasingly unrealistic. Even harder to swallow: whenever something on the network changed, an administrator had to recompile the HOST.TXT file and push it to every machine over FTP, which usually happened once or twice a week. That delay, too, was unacceptable.

Later, on November 23, 1983, Paul Mockapetris designed DNS and submitted RFC 882 and RFC 883 (later replaced in 1987 by RFC 1034 / RFC 1035).

Its core ideas can be summed up in a few points:

  • A consistent namespace: do not stuff network numbers, addresses, or routing information into names
  • Distributed maintenance: the full database cannot be stored centrally; it has to be sharded + cached
  • Delegated authority: whoever owns the data controls the update/cache policy
  • A general-purpose directory service: not just host addresses, but mailboxes and future unknown record types too

That guaranteed a decentralized distributed system (each organization could manage the naming of its own machines) that made updating the network easy.

The Prerequisite for www

We said earlier that every organization could manage its own machines, and that by allocating domain names for itself, an organization could divide up responsibilities very conveniently.

Although port technology had existed since 1980, allowing one machine to run multiple services, early machines were expensive and short on resources — you could not have a single machine handle both web service and mail service. So the early approach was to run different services on different machines, like this:

ftp.example.com    file transfer
mail.example.com   mail
news.example.com   newsgroups

That came with a number of benefits at the same time:

  1. Clear management boundaries — mail was the sysadmin's problem, the Web belonged to the newly formed network team; each side ran its own machines and no one had to take the blame for the other.
  2. Fault isolation — if the mail service went down, it could not affect the Web, and vice versa.
  3. The DNS design philosophy — the domain name system was a “hostname → IP” mapping from the very start, not a “service name → IP” mapping. You give each machine a name, and you call it whatever service it runs.

So www is essentially just a third-level domain, with no special privileges whatsoever.

The Arrival of www — 1989

In 1989, Tim (the person on the cover) proposed the concept of the World Wide Web at CERN. The point was not to lay down a website prefix and call on everyone to use www as the domain for web service; it was to propose the URL/HTTP/HTML hypertext system, so that documents could link to each other across machines and be published across organizations.

For instance, CERN's first web server used info.cern.ch, not www.cern.ch.

By the end of 1990, Tim had successfully launched the first web server and browser at CERN, proving that the ideas behind the proposal were workable. He wrote the relevant code directly on a NeXT computer and kept that server running in his office. To stop anyone from accidentally shutting the server down, he stuck a label written in red ink onto the computer: “This machine is a server. DO NOT POWER IT DOWN!”

But when the Web joined an existing network as a new service, administrators usually gave it its own hostname. ftp/mail/news and the like were already named after their services, so the Web carried on the pattern with www.

A Little of What Came After — 1990s

The popularity of the www naming may also have had something to do with the release of the Mosaic browser. In 1993, NCSA released Mosaic, the first browser that let the general public look at images and click links. NCSA's own web server was called www.ncsa.uiuc.edu. The bookmarks and sample links built into Mosaic all pointed at that address, so the first thing users around the world saw when they encountered the Web was www.

Then came Yahoo (1994), Amazon (1994), and eBay (1995), the first wave of commercial internet companies, and their new URLs followed the www prefix as well. That is how it became familiar to the general public.

Why www?

So why, out of all these names, www?

Someone once emailed Tim to ask exactly this; you can click the link to see Tim's explanation.

His explanation is quite interesting:

  1. www was something he “suggested,” not something he “mandated.”

“It is a convention. I suggested it early on, in this guide...”

He suggested it in a Style Guide (a guide written for webmasters) — that is, he wrote an article saying “you could do it this way.”

  1. Why not use the machine's own name?

“An alias was a better alternative to 'pegasus.foo.com' which typically resulted when someone who happened to have a machine called pegasus started to run a web server...”

What he means is: in the early days, plenty of people just grabbed whatever machine was at hand — one called pegasus, say — and ran the Web on it, so visitors had to use pegasus.foo.com. That name meant nothing; users could not remember it, and they could not tell what it was for.

So he suggested giving it an alias, www, so that one glance told you it was a web server.

  1. Why the three letters “www”?

Because the existing convention was already to name hosts after their service abbreviation:
He was simply fitting the Web into that existing naming scheme. www was not chosen because it was special, but because it followed the same pattern as ftp and mail.

  1. Why not just use the bare domain foo.com?

He gives two reasons:

“Typically early webmasters could not have comandeered the 'foo.com' address itself.”

Meaning: the bare domain foo.com is the “root identity” of the domain, usually controlled by the sysadmin, and the early Web people (webmasters) had no permission to change the DNS records of the bare domain. All they could do was add a subdomain within the area they could control.

“You don't have this flexibility of configuration if you point everyone at 'foo.com' itself for all services.”

The other reason is flexibility: with a www alias, if the web service grew later on, you could easily point www at a bigger machine without affecting the bare domain or the other services.

One Entertaining Detail

At the end of his answer, Tim says he is “of two minds about it now.”

Because by 1999, the Web had become the biggest service for many companies, and he thought maybe it was time to let the Web claim the bare domain. But he stresses at the same time: you can only pick one, you cannot run both as the main site, or your cache efficiency gets cut in half.

That is also in line with the idea in our next post, about why today's networks no longer use www and can just link to the bare domain instead.

items.title: FingerBlock: A Game Demo Built with AI
items.content_text: AI translation notice: This English version was translated from the original Chinese article with AI assistance. Some nuances may differ from the original. A while back, I happened to notice that a hand-tracking library I had starred on GitHub a long time ago had shipped an update. I have long since forgotten why I starred it — probably because I had just heard about hand tracking, thought it sounded cool, and hit the star button. I had never actually looked at it, or even read any of its code. But this chance glance got me thinking: so many years have passed, AI has come this far, hand tracking must be pretty impressive by now too. So I went to read up on it, found Google's MediaPipe, and quickly thought back to the motion games I played on the Xbox 360 as a kid. If I could build a game with this, it would be pretty neat. It was just a passing thought, but it kept coming back to me before I fell asleep. Then a concept for a rhythm game in the vein of Beat Saber slipped down the chimney of my mind like Santa Claus and left this gift behind: you face your laptop's camera, blocks in the game slide along tracks toward a judgment grid, and you hit them with your fingers. The controls are simple and easy to grasp, and it seemed reasonably easy to build, too. So I turned to AI, describing the requirements in my spare moments between practice problems, and five or six conversations later the first version existed. The AI overlord's power really does get more terrifying by the day. The project code is already on GitHub: MarkXuJQ/finger-block. This article records how I settled on the game's basic design, which technologies I picked, and a bit of the optimization work. The Basic Technical Structure of the Project FingerBlock is a browser-side Vite + React project, since I am fairly familiar with that workflow. Rendering uses React Three Fiber and Three.js, which I used to imitate a bit of Beat Saber's sense of space. Interface icons come from Lucide, simple and efficient. Next, on to the core of the game: Hand Tracking: MediaPipe Hand tracking uses the Hand Landmarker from Google's MediaPipe Tasks Vision. It provides hand keypoint detection, and I used it to turn the detection results into the input FingerBlock needs. The flow in goes roughly like this: After the camera starts, the MediaPipe WASM files and the hand model are loaded on demand. It tries the GPU delegate first and falls back to the CPU delegate on failure. It tracks at most two hands and reads the index fingertip keypoint of each hand, which is the eighth landmark. The camera feed shown to the player is mirrored, so the code swaps the left and right hand labels to keep physical left/right consistent with on-screen left/right. converts video coordinates into viewport coordinates, and maps them onto the 3×3 or 4×4 judgment grid. The coordinates get simple smoothing to reduce the jitter from frame-by-frame camera detection. At that point I figured that since I already had a way to take input from hand gestures through the camera, I might as well add touch control too, so the game could be played on phones as well. So I had AI fill in that feature too. It is worth mentioning, though, that on phones and tablets there is often noticeable lag because performance is not quite sufficient, so this part could probably be improved gradually later. Here is the general idea: The camera is not the only input method. The project later added a mode, where the mouse and touch can both operate directly inside the judgment area. Touch uses and pointer capture to track multiple fingers, and even when no new fires, a continuous presence loop keeps a Hold alive. A while back, I happened to notice that a hand-tracking library I had starred on GitHub a long time ago had shipped an update. I have long since forgotten why I starred it — probably because I had just heard about hand tracking, thought it sounded cool, and hit the star button. I had never actually looked at it, or even read any of its code.

But this chance glance got me thinking: so many years have passed, AI has come this far, hand tracking must be pretty impressive by now too. So I went to read up on it, found Google's MediaPipe, and quickly thought back to the motion games I played on the Xbox 360 as a kid. If I could build a game with this, it would be pretty neat.

It was just a passing thought, but it kept coming back to me before I fell asleep. Then a concept for a rhythm game in the vein of Beat Saber slipped down the chimney of my mind like Santa Claus and left this gift behind: you face your laptop's camera, blocks in the game slide along tracks toward a judgment grid, and you hit them with your fingers. The controls are simple and easy to grasp, and it seemed reasonably easy to build, too.

So I turned to AI, describing the requirements in my spare moments between practice problems, and five or six conversations later the first version existed. (The AI overlord's power really does get more terrifying by the day.)

The project code is already on GitHub: MarkXuJQ/finger-block. This article records how I settled on the game's basic design, which technologies I picked, and a bit of the optimization work.

The Basic Technical Structure of the Project

  • FingerBlock is a browser-side Vite + React project, since I am fairly familiar with that workflow.
  • Rendering uses React Three Fiber and Three.js, which I used to imitate a bit of Beat Saber's sense of space.
  • Interface icons come from Lucide, simple and efficient.

Next, on to the core of the game:

Hand Tracking: MediaPipe

Hand tracking uses the Hand Landmarker from Google's MediaPipe Tasks Vision. It provides hand keypoint detection, and I used it to turn the detection results into the input FingerBlock needs.

The flow in useHandTracking.ts goes roughly like this:

  1. After the camera starts, the MediaPipe WASM files and the hand model are loaded on demand.
  2. It tries the GPU delegate first and falls back to the CPU delegate on failure.
  3. It tracks at most two hands and reads the index fingertip keypoint of each hand, which is the eighth landmark.
  4. The camera feed shown to the player is mirrored, so the code swaps the left and right hand labels to keep physical left/right consistent with on-screen left/right.
  5. videoLandmarkToViewport converts video coordinates into viewport coordinates, and getLaneFromPoint maps them onto the 3×3 or 4×4 judgment grid.
  6. The coordinates get simple smoothing to reduce the jitter from frame-by-frame camera detection.

At that point I figured that since I already had a way to take input from hand gestures through the camera, I might as well add touch control too, so the game could be played on phones as well. So I had AI fill in that feature too. It is worth mentioning, though, that on phones and tablets there is often noticeable lag because performance is not quite sufficient, so this part could probably be improved gradually later. Here is the general idea:

The camera is not the only input method. The project later added a pointer mode, where the mouse and touch can both operate directly inside the judgment area. Touch uses pointerId and pointer capture to track multiple fingers, and even when no new pointermove fires, a continuous presence loop keeps a Hold alive. That way, even after the browser has been granted camera permission, the player can still switch to touch and finish a round.

Audio Analysis: Moving Audio Processing into a Worker

From a Fixed Chart to Automatic Generation

After finishing the hand-tracking feature, I had AI build a small sample with one fixed chart first, to test whether my idea was workable. The result was quite good: it caught my index finger position nicely, and the detection was reasonably accurate.

Once the fixed chart worked end to end, the content production problem showed up.

I do not own the rights to any music, and I do not have the ability or the time to hand-craft charts for a large number of songs. Doing it like other rhythm games, where someone has to manually mark timestamps, positions, and block types, would make scaling the game very expensive. But playing with just a fixed chart and no music at all would be pretty boring.

Then I thought of the Steam game Dead as Disco. I have never actually played it, but I had seen gameplay videos of it. It made me realize that I could try doing what that game does: build a set of music analysis, then generate charts automatically from the analysis results, and let players upload whatever music they like. Would that not be lovely?

The Implementation

Music import supports whatever the browser can decode: MP3, WAV, M4A/MP4, and OGG, with a limit of 80 MB per file and 12 minutes of duration. That should be enough for the vast majority of music — and anyway, playing a rhythm game alone for 12 minutes is tiring enough. The file is then decoded in the current browser through the Web Audio API's decodeAudioData().

The processing in analysis-core.ts is more complete than simply reading the BPM:

  • First mix multiple channels down to mono and resample everything to 22,050 Hz;
  • Compute overall RMS energy with a frame of roughly 50 milliseconds;
  • Estimate low-frequency energy from the result of a 180 Hz low-pass;
  • Generate a normalized energy curve and a waveform preview over time windows;
  • Find transients from the energy difference between the current frame and the preceding few frames — the moments that likely correspond to drum hits or clear attacks;
  • Analyze BPM and beat candidates with the Beatroot algorithm from music-tempo;
  • Split the song into three energy sections: quiet, normal, and peak;
  • Compute a confidence score from the beat match rate and transient coverage.

The music-tempo I used is a lightweight MIT-licensed BPM/beat analysis library. It is well suited to producing quick candidate results inside a browser Worker, but it cannot possibly get everything right for music with a weak beat, free tempo, or long stretches of silence, so the interface keeps the ability to manually adjust the BPM, the first beat, and the playback speed (0.5×, 1×, or 2×). In most cases, of course, it still locks onto most of the rhythm.

Automatic Chart Generation: Rule Constraints

chart-generator.ts uses a pseudo-random number generator with a fixed seed. The seed is derived from the song identifier, grid size, difficulty, BPM, and first beat together, so the same piece of music under the same set of settings will reliably produce the same chart, and only after you change the parameters do you get a new result. Maybe that buys a certain stability.

The generator reads beats, energy, and transients from the audio analysis results, then uses the easy, normal, and hard configurations to decide the sampling step, density, chord probability, Hold probability, and maximum travel distance.

Block colors are tied to musical features as well: downbeats or strong transients produce red accent blocks, ordinary blocks are blue, and some low-intensity off-beat events are marked as yellow optional bonus blocks. This keeps the game playable while also reinforcing the music's rhythm visually.

But the genuinely tricky part is that “random content still has to be playable with two hands.” A person has at most two index fingers, and wildly random blocks are certainly not something a human can clear, so I added several kinds of constraints to the project.

At Most Two Fingers Occupied at Once

First, the two index fingers are treated as the maximum number of inputs available at once, and the generator uses MAX_SIMULTANEOUS_NOTES = 2 to constrain the number of blocks within overlapping judgment windows. Even if two blocks do not share the exact same timestamp, as long as they fall in the same hit window they are treated as competing for the same two fingers.

Double hits are allowed on high-energy downbeats, but the generator also checks whether there are already enough blocks nearby, to avoid accidentally creating a third target that needs handling at the same time.

No Holds in the Center Cells

Tracks that approach from a distance in 3D make the central area an important visual reference. If a long-lasting block sits in the middle, it can cover the depth outline and also get in the way of the player watching the blocks that follow. So lane-rules.ts first defines a single center cell for the 3×3 grid and four center cells for the 4×4 grid, and beatmap.ts rejects any Hold located in those cells during validation.

This rule exists in both the generation stage and the final chart validation stage: the generator uses excludeCenter to avoid the center, while the validator prevents future hand-written or external charts from bypassing the generator and writing illegal Holds. That way the rule is not just a convention people “hope to follow” but a constraint enforced at the data layer.

A Hold Restricts the Other Hand

A Hold is not a long block that is judged only once at its start. After hitting the start, the player has to keep the same hand inside the corresponding cell; the project scores the sustain every 0.25 seconds and allows a brief tracking grace period of about 0.18 seconds. If the hand is released partway through, the points already earned are kept, and no extra Miss is recorded.

Because one hand is occupied by the Hold, the other hand has less room to move. The generator therefore:

  • Only generates Holds in non-quiet sections where the duration is long enough and the energy is not low;
  • Reduces the free hand's generation density to a fraction of the normal state during a Hold;
  • Places the free hand's notes on whole beats where possible and reserves longer beat gaps;
  • Limits the free hand's travel distance and prefers the opposite side of the grid from where the Hold is;
  • Leaves a recovery gap after the Hold ends, then gradually restores travel distance and density.

On normal difficulty a Hold lasts about two beats; easy is longer, and hard is shorter but denser. Double Holds appear only with low probability in sufficiently long melodic sections, and they are placed on opposite sides of the grid so each hand has a clear target. laneBlockedUntil also prevents new notes from being generated in the same cell before the Hold ends.

The Chart Still Has to Be Validated

Everything generated goes through validateBeatmap(): it checks the version, grid size, difficulty, song information, note ordering, note IDs, whether color and role match, whether Hold durations are valid, and whether notes in the same cell overlap. The generator is responsible for creating content, and the validator is responsible for making sure the content honors the data contract, which makes problems easier to spot when the rules are changed later.

Game Sound Effects: Building a Drum Kit from a Few Samples

In the age of AI, implementing the logic has become easy, but assets are still a hard problem. Fortunately there is a huge amount of CC0 open-source material available online. Since most music can sit on top of a kick drum (and music that cannot take a drum is not really suited to a rhythm game anyway 😄), it was natural to use drum kit sounds for the hit effects. Every sound source used is recorded in public/assets/ATTRIBUTIONS.md along with its origin, license, date obtained, processing applied, and SHA-256 checksum.

The current hit sounds come from five recordings on Freesound marked CC0: KEVOY's side stick and rimshot, TheEndOfACycle's closed hat and sub kick, and quatricise's shaker. The project used FFmpeg to trim them, fade them out, limit peaks, convert the sample rate, and encode them as Vorbis OGG; miss.ogg is a low-passed, low-gain low thud.

At runtime the six OGG files are not treated as six unrelated cues but layered like a drum kit:

  • A normal Hit plays the side stick;
  • Good adds a light rim on top of it;
  • Perfect layers in the closed hat as well;
  • Accent stacks an extra low kick;
  • Bonus adds the shaker;
  • Miss uses the separate low thud.

This design gives the different judgments a shared tonal anchor while still distinguishing feedback through the number of layers and the timbre. The music channel and the effects channel also each go through a GainNode on the AudioContext, so hit sounds do not drown out the music the user imported.

Final Tweaks and a Bit of Simple Design

Once the core logic worked, the remaining work was mostly repeated playtesting and fine-tuning: block movement speed, the sense of depth on the tracks, the position of the judgment grid, the smoothness of the camera cursor, the flash and shards on a hit, the score and combo on the HUD, the density at each difficulty, and the relative volume of music and effects.

Clock, Judgment, and Feedback

At runtime the game does not use a plain setInterval as its only clock. Music playback uses Web Audio's AudioContext and AudioBufferSourceNode, MusicClock records the start time and pause position within the audio context, and the game logic then computes block positions and judgments from that music timeline.

The judgment window for ordinary blocks is ±0.26 seconds: within ±0.07 seconds is Perfect, within ±0.15 seconds is Good, and anything else still inside the overall window is Hit. The base scores are 1000, 650, and 350 respectively, and red Accent blocks get a 1.2× base score bonus. Yellow Bonus blocks are not quite the same as ordinary notes you can miss; they play the role of an optional reward.

Hold sustain scoring is also written as a deterministic function: every 0.25 seconds it only consumes complete scoring intervals and clamps time at the end of the Hold. Even if the browser stalls for a few hundred milliseconds on some frame, you will not get a different sustain score just because of a different number of animation frames.

Hit feedback is generated in one place by judgement-events.ts, and the Three.js scene plays the flashes, expanding rings, wireframes, and shard effects that strengthen the sense of impact; the results page also plots a cumulative accuracy curve and the timing of Misses. The project also freezes the music clock and the Hold compensation logic when the page is hidden, so that after switching to the background and coming back, blocks do not all skip past the judgment area because the page was paused.

Of course, this part is pretty rough, because I feel the idea has largely been realized, and unless something special comes up I probably will not keep optimizing it.

Final Thoughts

A Playable Demo in a Day and a Half

From seeing the hand-tracking library update to finishing a runnable FingerBlock demo, the whole process took about a day and a half. And I was not sitting in front of the computer writing code the entire time: I spent a good chunk of it doing practice problems and watching lectures, and used my lunch break to hunt for open-source libraries and assets, study audio analysis methods, and keep playtesting and adjusting the generation rules.

To be fair, AI really did speed up getting this idea off the ground by a large margin. From scaffolding the project and tuning the audio-track parsing to stuffing in all those constraint rules, a lot of the tedious boilerplate now just requires me to think the requirements through clearly and hand them to AI, and it produces the whole thing in one go. All I have to do is check and verify.

AI Is Powerful, but This Quick Experiment Was Not All AI

I will not credit AI with the whole of this quick FingerBlock demo.

As I wrote in an earlier post, When Open Source Is Only a Prompt: I Found a Ridiculous New Way to Open Source, a few good prompts, a clear tech stack, and well-chosen links to assets are the real key to getting the most out of AI and improving efficiency.

AI can take on more and more of the concrete execution work, but that does not mean we should hand over our basic thinking and planning as well. Only by keeping those foundational skills can we judge faster whether an idea is feasible, find suitable open-source resources more accurately, and understand what the AI-generated code actually solved and what problems it left behind. Maybe that is the technical constant that has stayed unchanged from Web coding to today's vibe coding.

September 23

Uh oh. I get the feeling that if I did this again now, AI could do more, and do it better. This is a message I saw in a group chat, and these games really are playable.

items.title: The Story of Beautifying My RSS Feed Page
items.content_text: AI translation notice: This English version was translated from the original Chinese article with AI assistance. Some nuances may differ from the original. TLDR: Back in March, while I was building this site piece by piece, I got to the RSS subscription part and added a styling scheme to the XML file. I was quite pleased with it. Then, just two days later, the page that had been rendering just fine was suddenly down to nothing but the XML document tree again. Later I asked about it in Zhilu's blog community group chat, and Zhilu pointed me to Mayx's “XML Beautification After Google Killed XSLT”. After reading it, I rethought how RSS, Atom, and browser rendering relate to one another, and that is how the current version came to be. Why Beautify RSS at All Every blog should have a subscription entry point. Blog posts usually live on a personal site. You can of course read a web page at your own pace, but if someone wants to follow what you publish over the long term, they have to open your site every so often. If the reader uses an RSS reader, though, new posts appear in their subscription list automatically, and there is no need to open the site every day just to check for updates. Sounds great, does it not? But for someone who is not familiar with feeds, opening one and seeing a bare XML file would probably leave them baffled. So I figured: since a feed is meant for people to look at, I might as well make it look like a page while I am at it. And as for which of the two images below is the more intuitive one, that needs no explanation. The First Version This happened in early March, around the time the site first went live—the same stretch when I had just started adding subscription features. Looking back now, the Git history records it pretty clearly: February 28: added the feed dependency package and created the script generate-rss.js to automatically generate RSS, Atom, and JSON Feed files from the posts under the content/posts directory March 1: hooked up both RSS and Atom first, so posts could automatically produce feed files. Evening of March 1: added XSLT to the RSS feed for the first time. March 2: tried using to convert post content into HTML, and added cover images, summaries, and subscription links along the way. Afternoon of March 2: unified the feeds on Atom it felt like the easiest to implement and the most broadly compatible option, with JSON Feed as a possible follow-up added on 2026.10.4 , and moved the files into the directory. March 4: added a subscription page with cards, a background image, and a pop-up preview, so opening in a browser no longer gave you dry, bare XML. My thinking at the time was the same as most blogs that style their feeds: The script reads the posts under and generates an Atom file; the Atom file references at the top; after the browser receives the XML, XSLT transforms it into an HTML page with cover images, summaries, and dates. The result was simple and effective, so I merged it into the site quickly. I thought the whole thing was finally done. I was pretty happy the first time I saw it working. Click the RSS button below, open the feed link, and instead of a dense forest of XML you got a page that looked a lot like the style of my blog. And right about then, the plot twist I had coming arrived anyway. The Styling Scheme Suddenly Stops Working A few days later, I opened the feed link again, ready to admire my handiwork and see what else could be polished, only to find that the page I had built was gone. All that was left in the browser was the bare XML file. At first I assumed it was my own fault—maybe while I kept updating the site's content I had accidentally touched the script, or maybe, being up late, I had carelessly changed something in the script and broken the styled page. Then I wondered whether vibe-coding certain pages had caused Vercel to get the Atom MIME type wrong. Following my own experience and the possibilities the AI suggested, I checked the stylesheet path, the response headers, and the build output, and re-confirmed whether the XML file still had the instruction. Each piece looked right on its own, but put together, it just would not work. The styled page rendered in my local dev environment, but not in Chrome online. Maybe this is also a bit of proof that blogs still have some value in the AI era: only if people keep sharing on the internet can AI get enough information, and only then can it better help more people. At the same time, I regret the disappearance of XSLT as a technology. On a site made by a blogger I follow, you can see that many people are still holding on, wanting to preserve the tech stack they are used to. But which way the wheel of history will turn, we can only wait and see.
