These experiences were difficult to count within the university's evaluation system. Nobody gives you extra points for learning to cook, paying utility bills, cleaning a room, or organizing your own schedule. Yet I increasingly believe that independent living is itself part of university. It slowly changed me from someone whose life was arranged by others into someone responsible for maintaining my own order.

Growth does not always happen in classrooms, laboratories, or competitions. Sometimes it happens after tidying a desk in the early hours of the morning and realizing that you really can keep your life running, one small piece at a time.

No GPA Myth, but No Effortless Freedom Either

If I wrote only about the benefits, this article would become self-defense—an attempt to force myself to believe my own story.

The negative consequences genuinely frustrated me. Because I did not prioritize GPA, my final score was 3.97 out of 5.00, which looked less impressive beside the 4.0-plus GPAs of those ranked ahead of me. I missed the university's postgraduate-recommendation quota by only two places, with a very small difference in score. Had I improved a few minor-course grades, perhaps I would have gained another year to attempt something bolder. If I could do it again, I would certainly try to find a more delicate balance and avoid missing that opportunity. Yet I also understand deeply that, if time rewound, I would probably make the same choices I made then.

This is why I am now more cautious when talking about “rejecting Reward Hacking.” Rejecting a single metric is not the same as ignoring the rules; pursuing genuine learning does not excuse us from responsibility for results. The evaluation system has problems, but it also controls access to many opportunities. My GPA was not exceptionally high, but my reasonably good ranking and learning experience did, in fact, give me many opportunities. My father often tells me:

A person must understand the rules and make use of them. If you fail to understand the rules at all, you can pay an enormous price at a critical moment.

So I do not want to summarize these four years with the attention-grabbing but irresponsible slogan, “I refused to compete, so I was free.” More accurately, I was constantly making immature tradeoffs between freedom and opportunity, interests and metrics, long-term growth and short-term admission tickets. I still endorse some of those choices; others return at night as regrets.

I also regard those regrets as part of who I am now. They remind me that a genuinely good strategy for life cannot simply oppose an evaluation system for opposition's sake. It must understand the power of metrics while refusing to be completely ruled by them. As I learned in high school, you need to understand the knowledge itself and also why that knowledge appears on the exam.

What Exists Beyond Meritocracy?

These experiences almost summarize my university years: self-study, fitness, competitions, projects, renting an apartment, and countless hours “wasted” with friends that nevertheless became infinitely precious. They are quick to list, yet I vividly remember every detail, challenge, and stroke of luck. The train is almost at the station, so I should bring this article to an end as well.

Even after writing it, I still do not have an elegant answer. Four years at university helped me understand meritocracy's appeal more deeply: it is clear, direct, and comparable. It tells you where you rank and how to work toward the next step. For many ordinary people, it is also a relatively fair channel for upward mobility.

But I increasingly doubt whether it can serve as life's highest objective. When someone constantly confirms their value by being “better than others,” it becomes difficult to stop and ask: Does what I learned make me freer? Does what I create truly matter? Are my relationships with others more sincere? Am I learning to understand a larger world, or merely climbing inside an ever-smaller ranking table?

Perhaps life needs an objective better than meritocracy.

It should not deny effort, dismiss ability, or dress laziness up as enlightenment. But it should be broader than “beating other people.” It should have room for genuine learning, concrete love, understanding society, the joy of creation, physical health, and memories of living alongside the people around us. It should also make room for all those moments that no metric records but that truly help a person grow.

items.title: A Xiamen Food-Crawl Diary
items.content_text: AI translation notice: This English version was translated from the original Chinese article with AI assistance. Some nuances may differ from the original. In the blink of an eye, it was already time to graduate. Xiamen is a beautiful city and an exceptionally comfortable place to live: its warm, humid climate; clean and orderly urban landscape; distinctive Minnan architecture; all kinds of greenery; bougainvillea blooming everywhere; and its broad, pristine bays... All of this made the city feel precious to me and made leaving difficult. My only regret was that, over those four years, I did not have more time and opportunities to wander through Xiamen and get to know it properly. To make up for that regret, I invited a classmate out for one more food crawl before graduation. We went looking for small shops with character and a personal touch. There were pleasant surprises, and there were disappointments too. All the photos were taken on a phone and left unedited, so please excuse the quality, haha. PuKu Fresh Doughnut Specialty Shop Opening hours: 10:30–20:00 Address: Near the Jimei Ancestral Temple, Jimei District Price: The mochi doughnuts we ordered were ¥15 each We had originally come at lunchtime for sour-cream curry, only to discover that the shop did not open until 14:30. With that plan foiled, we had no choice but to look elsewhere. On our way back, we suddenly noticed this inconspicuous little shop. It did not even have a large sign; we only stopped because a sidewalk board happened to mention doughnuts. The shop was spotless and almost minimalist, with mostly wooden furniture. It felt simple yet warm—an ideal place to sit for a while and take a couple of photos on a sunny day. As the saying goes, “Life is bitter, so have some mochi. Hello everyone, I am...” Ahem. We ordered two matcha mochi doughnuts and one preserved-plum guava mochi doughnut. The texture was genuinely excellent. The inside was remarkably elastic, while the shell was crisp. When I bit into it, I could feel the gluten pulling with a satisfying resilience, but it was calibrated perfectly and never became awkwardly chewy 🥲. The shell did not crumble everywhere like an ordinary pastry, either. Instead, it cracked naturally as the interior stretched and clung to the dough, making that combination of crispness and bounce unmistakable in every bite. The fillings deserve an even closer description 😋. On a hot day, the center felt wonderfully cool, with a rich texture like ice cream on the verge of melting, but none of the unpleasant iciness of frozen food. The matcha was intense without the usual tea astringency. The preserved-plum guava filling was more delicate, carrying the clean sweetness of ripe guava and tiny pieces of fruit. Pressing it against the roof of my mouth with my tongue revealed a surprisingly rich series of textures and flavors, although I could not really taste much of the preserved plum. The dough itself was only faintly sweet; almost all the sweetness came from the filling, where it served as a background note supporting the matcha and fruit aromas. Even after the filling was gone, the fragrance left in my mouth lasted long enough for me to enjoy the rest of the doughnut. Xiangkou Braised Beef Noodles Opening hours: 11:00–14:00, 17:00–21:00 Address: First floor of Xianghe Plaza, near Tuihua Park, Siming District Price: About ¥45 per person After finishing the mochi doughnuts, we immediately called a taxi into Xiamen Island and switched our plans to this beef-noodle shop. It was hidden beneath a very old, nearly abandoned shopping center. Even the lettering on the building looked so peculiar that, for a moment, I thought the world had glitched. The shop was clean as well, but this one felt a little warmer. It was small, with five or six two-person tables inside and another two outside—only seven or eight tables in total. Refinement seemed to be its whole philosophy. The food arrived quickly, around seven or eight minutes after we ordered. We each had a bowl of braised beef noodles for ¥39. The menu labeled it “mildly spicy,” but there was no heat at all, which suited someone from the “cannot handle spice planet” like me perfectly. The noodles came with a small side dish of cabbage pickled in-house with vinegar and xiaomila chilies. It was refreshing and crunchy. The bowl did not look large, but it was surprisingly deep, and the portion was just right for both of us. Extra noodles cost money, though the standard serving was already sufficient. The broth was full-bodied, led by savory saltiness, with a faint sweetness and an almost imperceptible sour-spicy note when tasted carefully. It was exactly the classic flavor of proper braised beef noodles. The noodles were smooth, springy, and resilient. More importantly, they held onto the broth, so it never felt as though the noodles and soup were two separate things. The bowl also included softened lettuce and a soy-braised soft-boiled egg. The real star, of course, was the beef. As the writing on the wall proclaimed, “We use only fresh yellow cattle.” The beef flavor was especially pronounced, and the pieces were large. They had been stewed with excellent timing: the fibers were tender, nothing lodged between my teeth, and the seasoning had penetrated fully. The best part was the soft, almost sticky section in the middle—perhaps the center of the beef shank, though I am not certain. It elevated the texture and softened what might otherwise have been a slightly lean and dry cut. The web of gelatin inside could practically be pressed apart on the tongue. Wild Strawberry Free Market Opening hours: 11:00–20:00 Address: 176 Lujiang Road, Siming District Price: Main dishes felt like about ¥40 on average; desserts about ¥30 After the beef noodles, both of us were far too full and had failed to transform into David Day 大胃袋, “Big Stomach” . We wandered around the park until roughly 3 p.m., then arrived at Wild Strawberry, a place some of our classmates often visited. It is close to the First Pier and the Twin Towers; walk less than 200 meters west after leaving and you will reach Zhongshan Road. Travelers with time to spare may want to take a look. The shop was not small—it occupied two fairly spacious floors—but the owner had created a distinctive atmosphere. Every table, chair, and even decorative object was different. The rooms were packed with things, like an exhibition assembled from finds at a second-hand market. The whole place carried the owner's unmistakable personal style. The menu covered everything from full meals to desserts. We were simply too full to order mains, so we each picked a dessert, and even those portions exceeded our expectations. The pistachio gelato had the texture you would expect from authentic gelato. It was not overly airy and did not vanish the instant it entered my mouth. Pistachio provided the dominant flavor, with a few crushed nuts, while the relatively low dairy-fat content kept it refreshing rather than greasy. The “truffle” was essentially a black-truffle chocolate cake. A light layer of cream covered the outside, dusted generously with cocoa powder. The chocolate was slightly bitter and the cream sweet; eaten together, they reached a reasonably good balance. Even after all the desserts we had already eaten, it did not feel excessively rich. The black-truffle flavor was not especially obvious, although there was indeed a lingering aroma reminiscent of truffle oil. The coconut soufflé surprised me the most. Soufflés seem to have become a new online craze recently, with little specialty shops appearing everywhere. This one did not have the factory-made texture of a mass-produced dessert; it had not even set completely. When we split it with a fork, a faint, warm egg aroma rose toward my nose. Instead of the hollow airiness of something packed with improvers, it felt soft, springy, and substantial. Dipping it in the salted cream on the side cut through the richness. There were also tart mango pieces and mildly sweet coconut chunks. I did not dare try the bayberry. Cocoa Protagonist: Xiamen Chocolate Museum Opening hours: 10:00–23:00 Address: 20 meters west of the intersection of Zhongshan Road Pedestrian Street and Taishan Road, Siming District Price: Free It will not be the most educational museum you ever visit, nor the most beautiful, but it may well be the best-smelling museum you have ever entered. The museum was small, with only two floors, but it was filled with sculptures made from chocolate, ranging from tiny and delicate to large and impressive. Thoughtful price tags even told visitors how much they would have to pay if they damaged one 😂. Staff kept feeding us little snacks along the route. It is not worth making a special journey for, but since it sits on Zhongshan Road not far from Wild Strawberry, it makes a pleasant stop along the way. Tutou Bar Not Recommended Opening hours: 14:30–20:30 Address: Near the Jimei Ancestral Temple, Jimei School Village Price: About ¥80 per person At the very end of the day, we returned to the sour-cream curry we had originally planned to eat. We doubled back and arrived at this little shop. It was tiny and tucked inside an alley; anyone not deliberately searching for it would certainly miss it. There were only four or five tables. The decor followed the familiar formula of an internet-famous niche café—full of personality that somehow did not feel very distinctive. The owner was attentive: he found a storage basket for my backpack, placed it inside, and slid the basket beside me. Unfortunately, the food itself did not satisfy me, or at least did not justify its price. We ordered a sour-cream chicken curry for ¥45, a ¥55 pasta dish whose name I cannot remember that supposedly used a chili sauce made by the owner's mother, plus a pineapple slush and a sweet-milk slush for ¥30 each. Starting with the drinks, I had the pineapple slush. It tasted like an ordinary instant pineapple drink mixed a little weak and poured through a slush machine. Nothing about it stood out, and there is not much more to say. The curry, to be fair, tasted good. But for the signature dish, neither its flavor nor its character was particularly clear. The curry itself was mild, containing chopped and crushed chicken and irregular pieces of potato stewed until very soft. The potato had almost dissolved into the sauce, making it good for mixing with rice. The minced meat retained some texture and filled the sauce, while the chicken—probably thigh meat—was not dry. Yet the sour cream was so subtle that it added no especially distinctive flavor. You could easily spend just over half as much elsewhere and get curry rice of comparable quality. The rice was another major deduction: it lacked any rice aroma, did not contain enough moisture, and tasted utterly ordinary. Perhaps we arrived too late—the curry was already a little cool, and the rice had dried out as well. Finally, the pasta. We originally wanted the pesto pasta, but then came the classic “indie-shop owner” routine: “Have you had pesto before? If not, I would not recommend it to beginners. Most people will not like it. I recommend this one instead.” So we accepted the owner's suggestion. The menu called it handmade pasta, but the photo makes it obvious that it was not. Truly handmade pasta should not only have a shape better suited to holding the sauce; the egg-to-water ratio should also make it chewier, rather than giving it the same texture as supermarket pasta. As for the sauce, it had heat but no fragrance. There is a Chinese saying that serving food hot makes it taste three times fresher, yet even straight from the kitchen this sauce felt dull and left no strong impression. Besides being expensive, the portion was not enough to feed one person. Here are a few other photos from the trip to finish: And perhaps my university years deserve a speeding ticket too.

items.title: What Do Computer Science Majors Actually Learn?
items.content_text: AI translation notice: This English version was translated from the original Chinese article with AI assistance. Some nuances may differ from the original. Whenever I chat with the elders in my family, or introduce my major to younger students who are getting ready to choose one for the gaokao, I get asked the same question: What do you computer science people actually study? The question looks simple, but answering it clearly is not easy. Because the word “computer” is far too broad in everyday life, and for anyone with even a passing knowledge of technology, there are also far too many directions within it. If you have never studied the major yourself, plenty of misconceptions remain. Some people think studying computers means writing code, some think it means repairing PCs and installing operating systems, and others think it means making games, building websites, or doing artificial intelligence. All of these are related to computers, but each is only one direction within the field, and they have little to do with what “computer science” means in undergraduate education. Undergraduate “Computer Science and Technology” is mainly a complete system built around “how to make machines process information reliably, efficiently, and automatically.” It begins with mathematics to lay the logical foundation, then expresses everything clearly in code; but what matters most is the abstraction, systems thinking, engineering, and problem decomposition behind it all. So I want to write a simple user manual. Next time someone asks me “What do you study in computer science?”, I can just send them this article, which beats explaining it from scratch every time and still not being clear or complete. Of course, the curriculum differs from school to school, and I have never personally taken computer science courses at a top university. Fortunately, Berkeley and MIT publish many open courses, and through them I have caught a glimpse of how top schools think about education. What follows is mainly based on my own school—an ordinary first-tier university—and the content common to most domestic “Computer Science and Technology” undergraduate programs, plus what I learned from those open courses. First, a Misconception: Computer Science Is Not “Learning a Piece of Software” Many people's first impression of a computer science major is whether you can fix a computer, install an operating system, make a PowerPoint deck, or edit a video. These are certainly useful skills, but they are not the core of the major. Otherwise you would study mechanical engineering just to turn screws, architecture just to move bricks, and food science just to put chocolate chips on Chips Ahoy cookies. In undergraduate education, computer science mainly cares about: Why can a program run at all? How is the data inside a program organized and processed? How does the network move information from one place to another? Why can an operating system run many programs at the same time? How is a large system designed, developed, tested, and maintained? How do algorithms solve problems while using as little time and as few resources as possible? Next, I will also discuss mainstream directions such as artificial intelligence, databases, graphics, cybersecurity, and embedded systems, sharing what I have come to understand about them over the past few years and what problems each one is trying to solve. Now let us go bottom-up, layer by layer, through where the ideas of computing come from, what our learning goals are, and the problems and detours I ran into along the way. Layer One: Mathematical Foundations When we first entered university, many classmates were surprised: “Why am I majoring in computers, and the first thing I have to study is this much math?” During freshman year we would get together and complain about exactly this, but later on we realized that mathematics is not just the algebra from elementary, middle, and high school—that is called elementary mathematics. What undergraduates study is broader and deeper, and the foundations really do matter. Calculus, linear algebra, probability and statistics, and discrete mathematics are basically unavoidable. Some schools even cover numerical analysis, combinatorics, or operations research. Calculus focuses on continuous change and the ideas of differentiation and integration; linear algebra shows up constantly in graphics, machine learning, and data processing; probability and statistics underpin artificial intelligence, data analysis, and stochastic processes; and discrete mathematics is especially close to computing—sets, logic, graphs, trees, relations, recursion. These sound like mathematical concepts, but they keep reappearing later in data structures, algorithms, databases, compilers, and artificial intelligence. I happened to study discrete mathematics fairly seriously back then, and later it gave me a feeling of understanding one thing and grasping many others. Of course, there is no need to be intimidated. For an ordinary student who does not plan to keep struggling at the frontier of technology, there is really no need to push mathematics especially hard . Even if you forget most of it later, it will not affect your job search or your ability to handle ordinary front-end and back-end programming problems. Most undergraduate math courses are just cultivating a way of thinking, so that when you meet complex concepts later you are not completely without a handhold. The problems I ran into: Over my four years of university, if I had simply followed the school's courses step by step, I most likely would not have gained any deep understanding of mathematics. To make assessment easy to quantify, school courses do not test your mathematical understanding or your way of thinking; they mainly test your ability to solve problems. I think this is a problem with how schools assess students. Take the most telling example: almost every classmate around me understands linear algebra as computing determinants, multiplying matrices, finding eigenvectors... and not one of them thinks about its geometric meaning. My impression is that we focus too much on the “algebra” part of linear algebra and neglect the idea of “linear,” so that most students, even after studying artificial intelligence or graphics, do not understand why matrices have to be there I will put together a separate article about this sometime . Only by teaching myself Professor Gilbert Strang's 18.06 course and 3Blue1Brown's animated explanations did I begin to grasp the concepts and meaning of mathematics from the ground up. Layer Two: Programming Foundations Anyone who studies computer science has to be able to program 👋😭👋! The usual introductory languages are C, C++, or Python, depending on the school. The question looks simple, but answering it clearly is not easy.

Because the word “computer” is far too broad in everyday life, and for anyone with even a passing knowledge of technology, there are also far too many directions within it. If you have never studied the major yourself, plenty of misconceptions remain.

Some people think studying computers means writing code, some think it means repairing PCs and installing operating systems, and others think it means making games, building websites, or doing artificial intelligence. All of these are related to computers, but each is only one direction within the field, and they have little to do with what “computer science” means in undergraduate education.

Undergraduate “Computer Science and Technology” is mainly a complete system built around “how to make machines process information reliably, efficiently, and automatically.” It begins with mathematics to lay the logical foundation, then expresses everything clearly in code; but what matters most is the abstraction, systems thinking, engineering, and problem decomposition behind it all.

So I want to write a simple user manual. Next time someone asks me “What do you study in computer science?”, I can just send them this article, which beats explaining it from scratch every time and still not being clear or complete.

Of course, the curriculum differs from school to school, and I have never personally taken computer science courses at a top university. Fortunately, Berkeley and MIT publish many open courses, and through them I have caught a glimpse of how top schools think about education. What follows is mainly based on my own school—an ordinary first-tier university—and the content common to most domestic “Computer Science and Technology” undergraduate programs, plus what I learned from those open courses.

Many people's first impression of a computer science major is whether you can fix a computer, install an operating system, make a PowerPoint deck, or edit a video.

These are certainly useful skills, but they are not the core of the major. Otherwise you would study mechanical engineering just to turn screws, architecture just to move bricks, and food science just to put chocolate chips on Chips Ahoy cookies.

In undergraduate education, computer science mainly cares about:

  • Why can a program run at all?
  • How is the data inside a program organized and processed?
  • How does the network move information from one place to another?
  • Why can an operating system run many programs at the same time?
  • How is a large system designed, developed, tested, and maintained?
  • How do algorithms solve problems while using as little time and as few resources as possible?

Next, I will also discuss mainstream directions such as artificial intelligence, databases, graphics, cybersecurity, and embedded systems, sharing what I have come to understand about them over the past few years and what problems each one is trying to solve.

Final Thoughts

A computer science and technology major covers a lot, and it is scattered.

It has mathematics and engineering; theory and practice; it requires understanding the underlying systems and being able to build applications on top. When you first start, it is easy to feel that these courses have nothing to do with one another: math is math, C is C, operating systems are operating systems, databases are databases. But as you go further, you slowly discover that they are all answering the same question:

How can information be better represented, stored, transmitted, processed, and used?

This article is a very rough introduction, mainly as a record of what I have taken away from four years of continuous study, along with the problems I noticed and my most sincere advice. The learning experience of an ordinary student at a university outside the 985 and 211 tiers, who is full of uncertainty about the future, cannot cover everything, but at least I hope it helps parents and students interested in computers form a basic impression: computer science is not a pile of math, nor simply typing code. It is understanding every layer underneath the computer.

If you do choose to study it, you will most likely run into plenty of bugs that give you headaches, courses you cannot follow, environments that will not configure, and projects you cannot finish.

But there will also be some very happy moments: the first time a program runs, the first time a web page goes live, the first time a model produces a result, the first time a small tool you wrote actually helps someone. Those moments make you feel that you really are turning the ideas in your head into reality, little by little.

These tiny bits of happiness and positive feedback are probably what attracts me most to computer science.
items.summary: [AI-translated] For anyone who wants to know what a computer science and technology major actually studies: it is not just writing code, and not just fixing computers, but a whole course of training built around computation, systems, software, and engineering practice.

items.title: Why Do I Recommend College Students to Write Blogs?
items.content_text: After the gaokao, I came to a city 1,800 kilometers away from home for university. I walked out of the stage of life where exam scores were almost the only standard, and I encountered many things that made me start thinking. I also faced many choices that I had to make by myself. Sometimes one small thing would stay in my mind until midnight, repeating itself before sleep, leaving me with a stomach full of things to say. The next day, when I tried writing it down, I realized it was often just one or two short paragraphs of scattered thoughts, not much content at all. Writing helped me ease a lot of anxiety, and it also left clues for me to look back on later. Now when I turn back and read those records, I can clearly see how my worldview was pieced together from fragments of daily life. Writing a blog is a very good way to record these bits and pieces of life, making the origins of your thoughts traceable. As a College Student, What Can You Write About? The main audience of a blog is yourself. Many people do not write, and some are even afraid to write, because they think, "I'm not an expert, so nobody will read what I write." But the opposite is exactly why blogging is valuable. The most precious stage is precisely when you have not fully thought something through. Writing it down is itself a process of organizing your knowledge and the information you have. When writing, in order to express your thoughts, you gather related materials, check relevant content, and clarify the chain of logic. The goal is to squeeze that vague cloud floating in your mind into a visible shape. Actually, blogging does not have that many rules. You can record your hobbies, record the things that went wrong, and record the thoughts that make you feel "different" your "difference" is actually a clue and trace that helps people like you find you . You can also share your views on trending internet events. For example, regarding the recent popular "Jiahao" behavior, I feel it is a stage of life that may be embarrassing to look back on, but is still full of chaos and heat. Like the changes in adolescent thinking described in FLCL . There is no need to pick up a magnifying glass after growing up and start judging everything, suppressing the expression and emotions of teenagers who are still in adolescence. You can share knowledge you have learned: bugs and solutions from small projects you tinkered with, difficulties and challenges you encountered, how you completed an experiment, reflections after finishing a book, or experiences battling Linux. All of these can become small articles, like save points in life that you can come back to from time to time. How Do You Publish It After Writing? A blog is meant to be seen. Publishing it is like turning the sign at the door of a small shop to "OPEN," opening a door on the internet. Andy Matuschak calls this "working with the garage door up." Passersby glance inside, see you knocking things together, and naturally know someone is working here. If you have a bit of spare money, you can try buying your own domain name and use AI plus open-source projects to build a small website that fits your own taste. There are also many ready-made blog templates online. You can learn to adapt one, or directly deploy a site that belongs to you. If you do not want to deal with all that for now, you can simply write in any note-taking app and publish selected pieces to platforms with broad audiences, such as Zhihu, Bilibili, or WeChat Official Accounts. Good content will eventually find people willing to read it. As for things you do not publish publicly, you can keep them as your own archive, as clues to your thoughts. Looking back later is not a bad thing either. What Is a Good Blog Like? When it comes to what kind of blog counts as "good," I do not think you need to make it too complicated at the beginning. But there are a few points I want to talk about. The Audience of a Blog A blog is a public article once it is published, so you first need to consider the audience: who is reading it? Although I said earlier that the biggest audience of a blog is yourself, what you write should still have a certain public quality. It can be a place to clarify your own thoughts, but while you benefit from thinking and organizing, others should also be able to see something in it. The more professional and niche the topic is, the more you need to think about this. Of course, you can also use your blog like a "QQ Zone." Many bloggers dislike this concept and find it childish, but if your purpose is socializing and sharing, I do not think there is anything wrong with it. Through many similar personal blogs, I have seen the worries and joys of many peers like me. It feels like meeting a stranger who somehow becomes a friend. I think that is pretty nice. The Labeling of a Blog A blog should have its own theme. If a good blog wants to be remembered, it is best if people can easily attach a label to it. For example, when people want news analysis, philosophy reading notes, historical explanations, economic changes, or technical blogs, they can immediately think of whose website to visit. But this requirement is a bit too high for a college student. A normal college student, after coming out of the gaokao experience, usually does not have much life experience, deep reading, or even a writing habit beyond the style of exam essays. That is completely normal. When you have fewer topics to choose from, you can write as much as you can and record many aspects of your life. At this stage, you can use category management so that readers who need specific content can filter things simply. They can block out your daily fragments and focus only on your main output. This may be a passable solution. After you accumulate enough experience, it is not too late to open a dedicated column. I partly refer to the ideas of the 2750words blogger. I agree with most of his philosophy, though perhaps our life stages are different, or our entry points into blogging are different. I think a blog should still be centered on the blogger. Since it is already a personal blog, it is unreasonable to let someone else's design philosophy decide everything. If you do not like a website, you can simply choose not to read it. There will always be people who do like it. Just keep your own strong authorial presence. After all, the owner of the blog is you. Comfort will always matter more than being "correct." The Word Count of a Blog There should be some limit to word count. Many people do not like reading overly long articles, or rather, overly verbose articles. If a simple matter is hard to explain in fewer words, it probably means the writing is not clear enough yet. Verbose but unclear expression is a big problem. My advisor once gave me a requirement: "Your writing should have key points, so readers can roughly understand the intention within 30 seconds. It should have a two-minute reading path and a five-minute reading path." Proper bold text and well-designed section headings are fairly good ways to solve this problem. A Rational Discussion: Benefits and Costs I have said many things above, and it may sound like writing a blog is a "guaranteed profitable" deal. But if I do not tell you the corresponding costs and price, that would feel a little irresponsible. Writing a blog is not a social shortcut. It is more like opening a quiet little shop that few people visit. A good blog is a good way to speak on the internet. What you write represents the things you care about and the way you think about problems. But this does not automatically bring traffic, make your personal brand explode, make important people suddenly discover you, or bring opportunities on its own. Most of the time, blogging is slow cultivation by one person. From a personal perspective, maintaining and persisting with a blog is not something everyone can do. I have seen too many blogs disappear after the first three or five posts, sometimes even with the domain name no longer renewed. To be honest, I am also still in that "three-minute enthusiasm" stage, and future updates probably will not be as frequent as they are now. Also, "being misunderstood is the fate of anyone who expresses themselves." If you are sensitive, you will pay some emotional cost. Maintaining a website also requires continuous financial input. How it develops later is indeed hard to say. Blogging, as an activity that has already declined, does not bring many direct returns. We are now in the era of new self-media. Making videos and short videos is a more popular and mainstream choice. With platform support, there is more traffic and more visibility. Considering so many disadvantages, why do I still recommend it? First, as discussed earlier, writing articles is, so far, the fastest form of output, the one that most forces you to think, and the one that exposes logic most directly . What is truly valuable is the thought behind the words. Writing can greatly train a person's ability to think. Second, as a flexible form of output with low time cost, low storage cost, and a low entry threshold, writing has the highest cost-performance ratio among output-oriented hobbies. Pure text publishing is supported by many platforms, and a good article can be lightly modified into a video script, serving as the foundation for other forms of output. Create Boldly The confusion, awkwardness, sudden happiness, and unexplained sadness we are experiencing now are all gifts that belong uniquely to this stage of life. When we look back later, perhaps we will be grateful that we once made the decision to lay out our thoughts and record them. After all, in this empty space of the internet, only when you keep a light on will someone follow that light and come over to say: "Hey, I am here too." I am not sure how far this light can shine, nor how long it can stay lit. I simply believe that some things do not need to prove they are worth starting before they become worth starting.

items.title: Handy Little Tools for Surfing the Web
items.content_text: AI translation notice: This English version was translated from the original Chinese article with AI assistance. Some nuances may differ from the original. Let me start a post I can update whenever I like. There are some tools I really do want to recommend, but doing it one at a time feels too fragmented, so I will collect them here. If I come across new ones, I will keep this updated too! To make things easier for everyone, I will paste the original links as well. Immersive Translate In the internet age, multilingual education has gradually spread into compulsory schooling everywhere, and getting information across languages is easier than ever before. But a person's energy is always limited. Most of us can read content in two languages, and beyond that things start to get headache-inducing. Meanwhile, Chinese does not make up much of the information on the internet — according to Wikipedia's statistics, it ranks only tenth. The numbers are not exact, but they do say something. A lot of computer-related knowledge can only be found by searching in English. And information about the specific culture of a particular country is even more of a challenge. Rank Language Percentage ---- ---------- ---------- 1 English 59.3% 2 Russian 8.4% 3 Spanish 4.2% 4 German 2.9% 5 Turkish 2.9% 6 Persian 2.8% 7 French 2.8% 8 Japanese 2.4% 9 Portuguese 2.2% 10 Chinese 1.3% 11 Vietnamese 1.3% 12 Italian 1.0% At that point, having an effective translation tool — one that also lets you glance at the original for comparison — works like Zhuge Liang's feather fan and silk headdress: the channels through which you find information suddenly widen. Tampermonkey a.k.a. “Oil Monkey” This extension needs no introduction. It is basically a cheat code for your browser: by running scripts inside the browser, it unlocks new features or grants you entirely new ones! But there is a strange pattern — everyone knows this extension is powerful, yet few people actually use it. The reason is that they do not know what they need, or where they would need it, and when they go browse the script marketplace, everything they see is a feature they are unlikely to use. So here are a few that have worked well for me; you can give them a try. UserScript+--: The Script That Finds Scripts As the description says, it is a script for finding scripts. Run it on a site you visit often, and you can discover how many people have already added which features for that site. It is also extremely simple to use: just click the button on the extension and it jumps straight to a list showing the relevant scripts. The script is lightweight and efficient. I will paste the source code directly — it is already enough for me: Weibo, Zhihu, Bilibili, and Xiaohongshu Keyword Blocker Sometimes when you are browsing online, plenty of posts with particular keywords get pushed at you, and some of them are just there to stir up anxiety. With this extension you can cut down on some of that pointless anxiety, and you can add your own custom keywords too. Pretty good. Scripts That Lift Copy Restrictions There are actually plenty of scripts for this on Greasy Fork, and even on GitHub, or really anywhere on the internet, so I will not paste a specific link. It is genuinely useful — you can search for one yourself. Auto-Skip the Sponsored Bits on Bilibili There is a bit of a moral constraint around using this one — it might count as watching pirated content... But if you really hate spending your video-scrolling time on ads for used-phone recycling, massage devices, robot vacuums, and mite removers, maybe it is fine to use it in moderation? Anyway, I am not encouraging it; I am just leaving it here in case someone needs it. Wappalyzer: Shows the Tech Stack Behind a Web Page This one is quite fun. You can see what tech stack the page you are currently browsing uses and which JS libraries it runs. If you are just getting into front-end development, you can check what the sites you like are built with. Or when you see a cool animation effect, you can see exactly which animation library it uses. That said, I should be clear: Wappalyzer's results are best treated as technical clues. They are not the same as the site's real tech stack. For example, I really do use React, React Router, GSAP, Lenis, and Framer Motion, but WordPress and PHP are actually false positives. The main site is in fact a semi-static site built on Vite + React + TypeScript + Tailwind CSS, and it does not use the WordPress CMS or a PHP backend. As for why it misreads things, it probably has a lot to do with the fact that my link preview feature uses WordPress.com's mShots screenshot service. A friend once told me that most people are afraid to click a link they do not recognize, so I added that feature — it makes the interaction more interesting too. As for MySQL, my comment section uses Twikoo, and Twikoo uses MySQL to store comments. That is probably the reason. That is all I have written down for now. If you have tools to recommend as well, feel free to share them in the comments!

/* #eslint-disable no-undef */
(function() {
  'use strict';

  // ==============================参数配置
  let thisDomain =  document.domain.split('.').slice(-2).join('.').toLowerCase();

  // 检查域名对应的脚本数量
  let getDomainCount = function(domain) {
      let siteData = GM_getResourceText('siteData');
      siteData = JSON.parse(siteData);
      let count = 0;
      if (siteData.hasOwnProperty(domain)) {
          count = siteData[domain];
      }
      return count;
  };

  function goGreasyfork() {
      let url = `https://greasyfork.org/zh-CN/scripts/by-site/${thisDomain}?filter_locale=0`;
      GM_openInTab(url, {
          active: true
      });
  }

  function goOpenuserJS() {
      let url = `https://openuserjs.org/?q=${thisDomain}`;
      GM_openInTab(url, {
          active: true
      });
  }

Weibo, Zhihu, Bilibili, and Xiaohongshu Keyword Blocker

https://greasyfork.org/zh-CN/scripts/543102-%E5%BE%AE%E5%8D%9A%E7%9F%A5%E4%B9%8Eb%E7%AB%99%E5%B0%8F%E7%BA%A2%E4%B9%A6%E5%85%B3%E9%94%AE%E8%AF%8D%E5%B1%8F%E8%94%BD%E5%99%A8

Sometimes when you are browsing online, plenty of posts with particular keywords get pushed at you, and some of them are just there to stir up anxiety. With this extension you can cut down on some of that pointless anxiety, and you can add your own custom keywords too. Pretty good.

Scripts That Lift Copy Restrictions

There are actually plenty of scripts for this on Greasy Fork, and even on GitHub, or really anywhere on the internet, so I will not paste a specific link. It is genuinely useful — you can search for one yourself.

Auto-Skip the Sponsored Bits on Bilibili

https://chromewebstore.google.com/detail/%E5%B0%8F%E7%94%B5%E8%A7%86%E7%A9%BA%E9%99%8D%E5%8A%A9%E6%89%8B/eaoelafamejbnggahofapllmfhlhajdd

There is a bit of a moral constraint around using this one — it might count as watching pirated content... But if you really hate spending your video-scrolling time on ads for used-phone recycling, massage devices, robot vacuums, and mite removers, maybe it is fine to use it in moderation? Anyway, I am not encouraging it; I am just leaving it here in case someone needs it.

https://chromewebstore.google.com/detail/wappalyzer-technology-pro/gppongmhjkpfnbhagpmjfkannfbllamg

This one is quite fun. You can see what tech stack the page you are currently browsing uses and which JS libraries it runs. If you are just getting into front-end development, you can check what the sites you like are built with. Or when you see a cool animation effect, you can see exactly which animation library it uses.

That said, I should be clear: Wappalyzer's results are best treated as technical clues. They are not the same as the site's real tech stack. For example, I really do use React, React Router, GSAP, Lenis, and Framer Motion, but WordPress and PHP are actually false positives. A friend once told me that most people are afraid to click a link they do not recognize, so I added that feature — it makes the interaction more interesting too. As for MySQL, my comment section uses Twikoo, and Twikoo uses MySQL to store comments. That is probably the reason.

That is all I have written down for now. If you have tools to recommend as well, feel free to share them in the comments!

items.title: Looking at AI Through the Lens of Meme: Thoughts After Playing Death Stranding 2
items.content_text: Recently I finished the story of Death Stranding 2 . The abstractness of some of its performances shocked me. I could not understand why certain scenes were designed that way: why did people suddenly start singing here? Why did the villain perform the American national anthem at the end? And why was pizza kung fu so powerful? After doing some quick research, I suddenly realized something: this kind of game seems very hard to copy. Not only because of its gameplay, but even more because of its cultural expression. What Kind of Game Is Death Stranding? Unlike the game genres already on the market, it has its own new gameplay experience and worldview. It is not like the Assassin's Creed series, which has already formed a relatively mature AAA industrial template: a big open world, repeated outpost clearing, RPG-style equipment growth, question marks all over the map the question marks in The Witcher 3 were still pretty good , and static story cutscenes. It feels as if, as long as the budget, team, and production pipeline are big enough, you can make something that "looks about right" though I heard Ubisoft is remaking Black Flag, so I will still have to try it on hands . It is also not like Soulslikes, which have a very clear gameplay skeleton: bonfires, death penalties, stamina bars, boss design, fragmented narrative. Change the worldview and art theme, and players can quickly understand, "Oh, this has some Souls flavor." Nor is it like a linear AAA game that gives you as many cinematic shocks and exquisite level designs as possible within a limited route. Death Stranding is different. Its gameplay is new, its game concept is something I have never seen before, and the pleasure it brings has a very distinctive taste. Others can imitate its art, its long takes, its barren, absurd, realistic, or slightly mystical atmosphere. They can even make an identical "delivery game" or "infrastructure-building game." But it is very hard to truly reproduce the feeling it gives players. Because the core of the game is not a single system, but a complete experience: walking through the wilderness with cargo, planning routes, keeping balance, completing asynchronous cooperation or confrontation with strangers , slowly stepping out a path on what used to be a barren and rugged wasteland, all inside a self-consistent and rich worldview, in a work that has its own philosophical discussion and ideological expression. Games are interactive art, so let's talk about gameplay. If we only talk about gameplay, it seems a little boring. What it focuses on is the worst part of almost every open-world game: walking time. Most game companies keep optimizing fast travel so players do not spend too much time on the road and get tired. But Death Stranding makes this its main selling point. The game is basically about delivering cargo from A to B. Yet once you truly get into it and quietly sync with the game's wavelength, you find a strong stickiness inside this "boredom": climbing steep mountains, sneaking through watcher territory, drawing out and defeating BTs, building infrastructure along the road to make later deliveries easier, and finally delivering cargo to an NPC with zero damage, receiving likes and blueprints for new equipment. Everything you do on this journey, including the path you walk, can be synchronized into another player's world: maybe your infrastructure helps someone else, or maybe the simplest thing you leave behind is just telling others that this route can reach the destination. During the process, you feel the joy of getting new equipment and the sense of achievement that comes from forming "connections" with other players. Its worldview also reaches a clever kind of balance. Timefall, umbilical cords, the Beach, the chiral network: a series of new terms and settings relate to each other while also corresponding to meanings in the real world, creating certain metaphors that make the world easier to understand and enter let me complain here about the long-winded text and so-called "setting terms" in some gacha games . All settings participate in the difficulties and challenges players encounter: some as special mechanics, some as final goals, and some as potential dangers that need to be guarded against. Meanwhile, Kojima-san also adds many Easter eggs into this world, or you could say "humorous and abstract" content, just like the performances I mentioned at the beginning. At first they made me wonder: won't this break the carefully designed worldview? For such a high-budget AAA game, is it not too risky for the director to smuggle in so much personal taste? But the result is just like the line circulating online: "Commercialization is under pressure, and finally yielded to Hideo Kojima." For casual players, these moments bring a knowing smile during the game. But if you dig into them carefully, you find that they not only do not break the worldview, but add another layer of metaphor and philosophical thought to it. The appropriately abrupt feeling hooks players into thinking. While feeling surprised, they can also experience the corresponding meaning. Whether you understand it or not, you slowly accept this abruptness, and it becomes one of the game's unique features. So I started to wonder: what kind of game creator is Hideo Kojima exactly? Why does he have so many fans around the world? Why does he dare to invest so much money into making a game that looks "not in line with the blockbuster formula"? Why was the first game so divisive when it first came out, while by the second one, many players could already seriously discuss it as a Game of the Year candidate? What Meme Means With this curiosity, I watched some Death Stranding 2 lore analysis videos on Bilibili and read some interviews with Hideo Kojima. I learned about a turbulent life experience full of misfortune and coincidence, one that carries the shadow of many otaku boys. I also learned how movies, games, reading, and thinking inspired his creative career. One interview especially caught my attention: when talking about his first directed work, Metal Gear , he said it mainly explored Meme. When I first saw the word, my immediate reaction was: how could "meme images" have been a subject of discussion nearly forty years ago? After all, in today's internet context, the most common Chinese translation of "meme" is basically "funny image template": cats and dogs with captions, reaction images, abstract templates. They all seem to count as memes. But the Meme Kojima was talking about was clearly not that. So I looked it up. According to the Wikipedia entry on Meme, the concept of the meme comes from Richard Dawkins's 1976 book The Selfish Gene . Dawkins wanted to express that culture also has units of transmission similar to genes. A meme can be a melody, an idea, a slogan, a fashion, a skill, or any cultural fragment that people imitate, copy, transform, and continue spreading. In other words, a meme was not originally an internet reaction image. Reaction images are certainly memes, but memes are much bigger than reaction images. Our two-part allegorical sayings are memes, idioms are memes, books are memes, movies are memes, internet catchphrases are memes, collective repetition in Bilibili comments is a meme, gamer slang is a meme you are not qualified, you are not qualified, and because of that you are not qualified , and even certain creative methods, aesthetic tastes, and narrative formulas are memes. Like genes inside culture, they are copied, rewritten, sometimes misunderstood, then recreated by generation after generation, and they keep living. AI Cannot Create Cultural Genes After understanding what meme means, and then thinking about the story design and hidden metaphors behind Death Stranding 2 , I could not help connecting it to the hottest concept of our era: AI. Suddenly, the whole thing became interesting to me. Today's large language models are not truly people with lived experience. They do not have blurry childhood memories, the joy of staying up all night playing games, the surprise of walking into the wilderness for the first time, or the feeling of being struck by a lyric or a melody late at night while emo. In essence, they are huge probability calculators, absorbing a vast amount of text, images, code, music, and knowledge left behind by humans, then searching for vector relationships among those existing materials and giving an answer that is "most like something a human would say." In other words, through a massive amount of human corpus, AI has already become very good at using existing memes. Ask it to write a cyberpunk story, and it knows how neon lights, rainy nights, prosthetic bodies, monopolistic corporations, and lower-class districts should be combined. Ask it to design a Soulslike game setting, and it knows roughly what ruined kingdoms, lost gods, curses, bosses, and obscure item descriptions should look like. Ask it to make an "internet-style" image, and it also knows the common templates in contemporary aesthetics. But the problem is that most of this is still calling, stitching, and redistributing existing cultural genes. AI can quickly rearrange the familiar things we already know, sometimes beautifully, completely, and convincingly. But New Cultural Currents Often Come from Bold Attempts and Mistakes Looking back at new cultural currents in human history, quite a few impressive ones came from a bold attempt, a misunderstanding, or simply an accident. Take the Renaissance as an example. Some ancient Greek and Roman knowledge of philosophy, literature, art, and science had been preserved, filtered, and used by the Church for theological purposes during the Middle Ages, partly to consolidate its rule and class structure. During the Renaissance, humanists such as Petrarch and Boccaccio rediscovered a large number of classical texts from the Arab world and monasteries. But they did not simply restore them in a fundamentalist way. Instead, they interpreted them through the eyes and needs of their own time . They emphasized the praise of human reason, secular life, and bodily beauty in classical culture, while to some extent ignoring or downplaying the superstition, slavery, and pessimism that also existed in antiquity. This created a historical and cultural explosion. Even Confucianism, which we now sometimes criticize as part of feudal tradition, was also an incredibly rebellious existence in its own social context. AI only produces something that is highly likely to be correct based on existing memes, or cultural content. The difference already appears at the level of underlying logic. So if you ask whether it can create a truly new meme, whether it can continuously create a new mode of expression, a new structure of experience, or a new "cultural gene" that humans will understand from then on, I still feel somewhat doubtful. That brings me back to why the performance arrangements and gameplay design of Death Stranding feel so precious to me. It does not simply invite Hollywood actors, shoot a pile of luxurious cutscenes, and then stuff them into an open-world gameplay loop everyone already knows. It did invite recognizable actors such as Norman Reedus, Léa Seydoux, and Mads Mikkelsen, and it does have cinematic shots, music, and narrative ambition. But it does not treat these things merely as gimmicks to make money. Instead, it uses a very strange, risky, and unstable gameplay system to push a new experience in front of players. "Delivery" is such an ordinary thing, even boring-sounding. But in Death Stranding , it becomes a way of connecting people. What you carry is not just cargo, but also weight, responsibility, route choice, risk, and time. A bridge you build may be used by another player you will never meet. A charging station you place may just happen to save a desperate player. The game's "connection" is not a line of dialogue. It is built into terrain, physics, resources, and asynchronous multiplayer systems. Even when I continued building facilities later, I started thinking about whether this device would still help other players after entering their worlds. This feels very much like the birth of a new meme. Before it, it was hard to imagine that a big-budget game could turn "walking" and "delivery" into the core experience. After it, whenever people see similar asynchronous assistance or confrontation, they may say: "This feels a bit like Death Stranding." That sentence itself shows that it has already become a cultural unit that can be recognized, quoted, and spread. From now on, there are two kinds of people in the world: those who have not played Death Stranding , and those who have. As for the bizarre performance effects mentioned earlier, I think it is precisely these bizarre performances that, in return, become strange memes. They give this distinctive game an additional kind of "connection" with other cultures and fans, and create new memes belonging to its own players, like a secret key for connection among the game's fans. From Another Angle, the Relationship Between AI and Meme May Not Be So Pessimistic If AI only keeps repeating old memes, then of course it will make culture more average, more similar, more "correct but boring." We can already see this flavor in many places: copy that is as pretty as a template but stiff, images that are as polished as templates but incomplete, and expressions that are fluent but lack personal experience. They are not bad, but they are also unlikely to leave long-lasting traces. But from the opposite direction, AI may also become a tool that helps memes keep growing. In the past, when someone had a strange idea and wanted to turn it into a game, animation, software, short film, or other cultural work, they often needed a lot of money, a team, technical accumulation, or the ability to absorb trial-and-error costs. Many ideas were not worthless; they died before they could land. Modeling, programming, art, sound effects, editing, testing: these are not merely "repetitive labor," but they really are high walls that must be crossed before an idea becomes a work. If AI continues to develop and can truly reduce costs in modeling, code, animation, scripts, level prototypes, and other parts of the process, letting more people bring their ideas into reality with smaller teams, less money, and shorter trial-and-error cycles, then that might be a beautiful thing. My own little website also developed this quickly and gained this many effects precisely because of AI. Because culture is not created only by big companies and big budgets. Many new memes may begin as one person's strange thought, a small team's obsession, a gameplay idea that does not look very commercial, or a simple sentence: "I just want to try whether this works." If AI can drag these thoughts out of people's heads and into reality, allowing more works that previously had no chance to take shape to be seen, then it is not replacing culture. It is widening the entrance through which culture can happen. Of course, the premise is that we still provide something truly human. AI can help us reach the work faster. But new memes may still have to grow out of human loneliness, curiosity, stubbornness, failure, and experience. The inspiration Death Stranding 2 gave me is probably this: when a creator truly presses their feelings, aesthetics, and sense of problems into a work, it has the chance to become a new cultural gene. At first, people may find it strange, alternative, or unlike a "normal game." But as long as it really strikes something, it will be remembered, discussed, imitated, or misunderstood, and then it will keep spreading. Finally, I want to use the closing words Hideo Kojima gives to players in Death Stranding 2 to look toward our future and development in the AI era. Even if we do not know what the future will be like, we should not stop exploring, and we should not stop trying. Though the future is a product of every present that precedes it, Tomorrow does not belong to today. To live is to imagine ourselves in the future. And there we inevitably arrive Yet our place in said future may not be the one we envision. -- Kobo Abe, The Search for the Present
