Finally, I want to use the closing words Hideo Kojima gives to players in Death Stranding 2 to look toward our future and development in the AI era. Even if we do not know what the future will be like, we should not stop exploring, and we should not stop trying.

Though the future is a product of every present that precedes it,

Tomorrow does not belong to today.

To live is to imagine ourselves in the future.

And there we inevitably arrive

Yet our place in said future may not be the one we envision.

-- Kobo Abe, The Search for the Present
items.summary: After finishing the story of Death Stranding 2, I began to understand MEME as a way for the genes of human culture to keep growing. AI can reuse these cultural genes, but new cultural genes may still have to grow out of human experience.

items.title: From Student Innovation Project to Graduation Thesis: How My Research Thinking Evolved
items.content_text: After finishing my graduation project, I kept wanting to write a blog post about it. I do not want to rewrite my thesis abstract. If I did that, it would be better to just read the thesis. What I want to record is how the project actually grew: at first it did not even have a clear direction. It was only an ordinary attempt to ask my advisor whether there was a suitable project I could join. Later, step by step, it became a student innovation project, a system, an algorithm, and finally my undergraduate graduation thesis. Looking back now, the most interesting part is not that I eventually built some amazing model or algorithm implementation. It is that I clearly felt, for the first time, that failure in research or engineering is not a full stop. It is a concrete signpost, telling me where to go next. The Starting Point: A Challenge In the second semester of my sophomore year, I went to my undergraduate advisor and asked whether there was any project suitable for me to participate in, partly because a senior strongly recommended that I try applying for a student innovation and entrepreneurship project. At that time, I did not have a clear idea of "medical imaging" yet. My understanding of "segmentation" was still roughly: circle out a certain region in an image, just like those classic YOLO examples from introductory computer science courses. My advisor introduced me to the PENGWIN 2024 pelvic fracture segmentation challenge, and asked me to first try exploring around this competition. PENGWIN's task is very intuitive, and also very difficult: given CT or X-ray data from patients with pelvic fractures, let an algorithm automatically segment the fracture fragments. The public description mentions why this type of task is hard: the pelvis has a complex structure; fracture fragments vary greatly in shape and location; and fracture surfaces often become blurry due to collision, compression, and adhesion. This was already close to the frontier of the field. For a complete beginner like me, it was extremely hard to even get started, not to mention that I still had ambitions to make something "innovative." The training set for PENGWIN Task 1 on Zenodo contains 100 CT cases with labels. The full dataset comes from 150 patients, with 50 cases reserved as the official test set for final scoring. The data clearly annotates the sacrum, left and right hip bones, and their fragments, with detailed descriptions. It was an ideal dataset. Back then, I did not truly feel the weight of those difficulties. My first reaction was more like: since there is data, a competition, and a task, let's build the system first. And so the student innovation project that "tortured" me for a whole year began. That year, several teammates and I built a basic medical management system. The system itself needed to handle data management, model invocation, and result visualization. It sounded like a complete project, and in practice it really did take a lot of time. Frontend, backend, data flow, model APIs: many things were written while searching, rewritten while learning, and overturned while building. Very often we worked until four or five in the morning before realizing we really had to rest. The hardest part of the whole process was team collaboration: explaining task requirements, expected outcomes, and so on. That development experience with teammates also exhausted me quite a lot maybe I will write another article about that later, but it is not the focus this time . By the midterm stage, the system finally had a basic shape, but my advisor pointed out a more important issue: the system could display results, but our medical image segmentation algorithm also needed innovation. Directly using other people's work was not enough for a student innovation project. That sentence hurt a bit. After slowly grinding out the system, it is easy to mistakenly believe that most of the work is already done, at least because the visible workload is clear. But in medical image segmentation, the interface only "serves the result." The truly difficult part is where the result comes from. And that hidden workload is much harder to explain clearly to others. My First U-Net, and My First Failure That was when I officially started filling in my knowledge of medical image segmentation. Naturally, the first thing I could not avoid was U-Net. It is a classic encoder-decoder structure in medical image segmentation. One side downsamples to extract semantic information, the other side upsamples to recover spatial details, and skip connections bring shallow texture information back in between. It did not sound too complicated, so I naturally developed a naive confidence: then I will write one myself. So I hand-wrote my first U-Net. Looking back now, that was probably one of the most educational pieces of code I have ever written. The model could run, the loss would drop, and the results could be visualized. Seeing my GPU fully occupied, the terminal reporting a new round of training information, and the loss curve slowly going down was honestly a very happy thing. But the results were still poor. Later, I tried adding small modules such as depthwise separable convolutions, spatial-channel dual attention, and SE blocks. At that stage, I had read very few papers. More often, I picked things from existing modules that "looked possibly useful," stuffed them into the network, and then listened to AI's flattery, feeling that I had done a decent job. The results did not suddenly improve just because there were more modules. There was some improvement, but still not enough. What was more brutal was that it still could not beat the competition baseline. That hit me hard. I had spent a year building the system, modifying the model, staying up late for months, and even abandoning fitness I was genuinely afraid of sudden death , but the final algorithmic effect was not ideal. That was the first time I realized deep learning does not automatically become stronger by stacking a few "advanced modules" together. Especially in medical imaging, data volume, annotation strategy, preprocessing, loss functions, post-processing, and evaluation metrics may each be more important than "adding another attention module." It was exactly this failure that pushed me toward the real problem of my graduation project: do not rush to invent a complex network. First understand why a strong baseline is strong, and then see where there is still room for improvement. Relearning from nnU-Net During the graduation project stage, a senior helped me reproduce nnU-Net. This step was crucial. What makes nnU-Net powerful is not only its network structure, but the way it systematizes a large amount of "engineering experience" in medical image segmentation. It automatically configures preprocessing, patch size, network topology, training strategy, and post-processing according to the properties of the data. So in many cases, it is not just an ordinary baseline, but a very solid segmentation pipeline. The nnU-Net paper also mentions that it can outperform many specially designed methods across multiple public medical segmentation tasks without heavy manual tuning. After reproducing nnU-Net, I finally had a more reliable reference. Then I read work related to FracSegNet. Instead of directly segmenting everything inside the full CT volume, it decomposes the task into two steps: first locating the left hip bone, right hip bone, and sacrum, then segmenting major and minor fragments inside the target bone regions. It also introduces a fracture distance map, or FDM, which makes the model pay more attention to regions near fracture contact surfaces. This idea inspired me a lot. The most troublesome part of fracture segmentation is often not whether the whole bone can be segmented, but whether a tiny gap between neighboring fragments gets filled, whether small fragments are missed, and whether strange false positives appear near broken ends. The overall Dice score may already look very high, but if two bone fragments that should be separated are stuck together by the model, the spatial relationship in 3D reconstruction and preoperative planning becomes completely different. In other words, this task does not need "roughly similar." It needs "the local structure must not be messed up." The New Paper from March Just after I finished reproducing nnU-Net and FracSegNet, while I was still worrying about how to improve further, my advisor gave me a new paper from March. The method was called SCNP, short for Same Class Neighbor Penalization. The starting point of the paper is clever: many segmentation models perform well on the overall region, but cannot guarantee accurate topology. For example, thin structures may break, small regions may appear out of nowhere, and originally separated structures may become stuck together. SCNP does not redesign the network. Instead, during training, it performs neighborhood propagation on logits: foreground positions are affected by weaker responses among same-class neighbors, while background positions are affected by more confusing responses among same-class neighbors. Intuitively, it means the model cannot pass by only predicting the center voxel well. It also needs to care about the most error-prone places among nearby same-class neighbors. This idea immediately matched pelvic fracture segmentation. The problem of fracture fragments is exactly a local structure problem. A narrow gap being filled, a small fragment being swallowed, or a false positive appearing near a broken end are all typical cases where "the large overall region looks fine, but the local connection relationship is wrong." SCNP also has an attractive engineering property: it mainly changes the logits before loss calculation during training. It does not require changing the inference process, nor does it require redesigning an entire complex network. However, directly applying SCNP to pelvic CT also carries risks. CT has noise, and there are stable bone regions far away from fracture surfaces. If neighborhood propagation is applied everywhere, it may amplify local errors in irrelevant regions too. So my graduation project made a compromise: combine the FDM idea from FracSegNet with SCNP, using the fracture distance map as a spatial gate so that SCNP acts more strongly near the high-risk fracture contact surfaces. In one AI-style sentence: do not make the model nervous across the whole bone; make it more serious where things are truly likely to go wrong. What My Graduation Project Actually Did In the end, the core of my graduation project can be summarized into three things. First, I reproduced and organized the baseline pipeline for pelvic fracture CT segmentation. The experiments used nnU-Net as the unified framework, comparing Max-flow, standard nnU-Net, the reproduced FracSegNet baseline, and different SCNP variants. The labels were also reorganized into three semantic classes: background, major fragments, and minor fragments. Second, I introduced SCNP neighborhood structure propagation before loss calculation. It does not change the inference structure of the network. During training, it makes locally difficult regions participate more directly in optimization, thereby complementing the insufficient constraints of CE + Dice on fragment boundaries, small gaps, and local connectivity. Third, I combined FDM and SCNP into a gated version. FDM-gated SCNP concentrates structural propagation near fracture surfaces and reduces unnecessary propagation in stable bone regions or noisy areas. In the experiments, I roughly compared different receptive fields and gating thresholds, and finally found that was a relatively balanced setting. Under unified local post-processing and the same evaluation protocol, FDM-gated SCNP achieved more balanced results compared with the reproduced FracSegNet baseline: All DSC reached , All LDSC reached , All HD95 was , and IoU was . Compared with the FracSegNet baseline, HD95 decreased by about , and IoU improved by about . Of course, these numbers should not be understood as "the problem is solved." There are no such easy victories in medical imaging. They are more like evidence for a small and specific point: on top of a strong baseline, if the training objective is pushed a little toward local structure, the model can indeed become more stable in boundary distance, local Dice, and fragment separation quality. Beyond the Results: What I Really Learned The most useful part of this graduation project was not a certain metric, but the way my understanding of "innovation" changed. At first, I thought innovation meant adding modules, changing structures, and drawing a more complicated network. Later I realized that in a real task, innovation is sometimes the opposite: explaining the problem clearly. Is the whole segmentation inaccurate, or are local boundaries unstable? Is model capacity insufficient, or does the loss function fail to punish the truly important errors? Do we need a larger receptive field, or do we need to constrain the propagation range? My first U-Net did not beat the baseline. That is certainly nothing to brag about, but it forced me to admit that my understanding of the task was too shallow. Later, reproducing nnU-Net and FracSegNet showed me that strong methods are not strong out of nowhere. They consider data organization, label design, training strategy, post-processing, and evaluation metrics together. Finally, introducing SCNP was not because it sounded new, but because it happened to respond to the recurring local structure errors in this task. From the student innovation project to the graduation thesis, this project felt like taking a long detour. At first I wanted to build a system, then I realized the algorithm behind the system was not good enough. I went on to modify the model structure, then discovered that casually adding modules was meaningless. I began reproducing strong baselines, and only then gradually saw the real problem. Finally, I returned to a very small change: during training, let the model look more carefully at the hardest nearby region. Maybe this is what a graduation project is for. It does not necessarily make you build something that changes the world, but it lets you go through a complete learning process with frustration included. You learn how a result comes into being, and you also learn why it is still not good enough. Problems That Are Not Over Yet Of course, this work still has many limitations. The current label space is still a three-class semantic segmentation of background, major fragments, and minor fragments. It cannot truly output an instance ID for every individual fragment. For complex multi-fragment cases, especially very small fragments, unified post-processing may still miss or merge fragments. FDM gating also depends on task priors. The threshold and receptive field mainly come from experimental selection and have not yet become an adaptive mechanism. More importantly, improvement in segmentation metrics does not mean clinical value has been fully validated. If this work continues in the future, the results should be put into downstream tasks such as 3D reconstruction, reduction planning, and surgical path design, to see whether improvements in local boundaries can bring real benefits to the workflow. But at least for me, this graduation project has already completed its most important task: it took me from "can it run?" to "why design it this way?" It also let me truly understand for the first time that the hardest part of an algorithm project is often not writing the network, but finding the errors worth optimizing. PENGWIN 2024 Challenge Description PENGWIN Task 1 Dataset PENGWIN 2024 Challenge Report nnU-Net Paper FracSegNet / Multi-scale Distance-weighted Pelvic Fracture Segmentation SCNP Paper

items.title: Four Years at University, and a Few of My “Little Drawers”
items.content_text: AI translation notice: This English version was translated from the original Chinese article with AI assistance. Some nuances may differ from the original. I have always loved surfing the internet and collecting all kinds of strange and wonderful websites and sources of information. Sharing them back and forth with classmates brought me plenty of new ones, and over time they became a shared language among us. My four years of university were, I would say, the four years in which I grew up the fastest socially: I went through a lot and saw a lot. Everything I want to share in this article is something I have been reading all along, and they are the sources I genuinely like. If you have any of your own you would like to share, please leave a comment below! 👏 Tech News Ruan Yifeng's Web Log Teacher Ruan's blog is probably the best known and most familiar of all Chinese personal blogs, and the “Technology Enthusiast Weekly” on this site has become a Friday ritual that many people myself included never miss. It is not confined to pure technology; it reads more like a general-interest magazine for the digital age. It covers the author's observations and thoughts on technology, tech news, excellent articles, new tool recommendations, digests, interesting comments, and more. Add the cover image and introduction the author carefully picks each week, and the content is remarkably rich 🤩—enough to serve as a weekly roundup of tech highlights. My favorite part is the author's tech observations, which are full of interesting thoughts and insights and often leave me feeling as though my cerebral cortex has been swapped out for a new one. Then there is the article recommendation section: I can honestly say that it is mainly through this weekly that I have come across many excellent personal bloggers and fresh ideas the kind that set trends! . Chaping's WeChat Account Updated at midnight sharp every night, Chaping is more like a “tech midnight snack.” On the many nights I was busy fixing bugs 🥱, I would open it at midnight for a bit of diversion. It skims quickly through the day's important little tech news, mostly the stuff closely tied to us users. It also runs short analysis and discussion pieces on whatever topics are currently hot. Chaping's main distinguishing feature is the way it explains hardcore tech news and business developments in very plain language laced with internet memes. The interactions in the comments are usually full of jokes too, and it even has a Daily Joke and an interactive section that gets discussions going in the comments, loosening the nerves wound tight by the day. Hacker News This is a minimalist tech community run by Y Combinator, and an important window through which I get “raw information.” For me, what draws me in most is its ranking algorithm: $$ Score = \frac{P - 1}{ T + 2 ^G} $$ where, $P$ is the entry's score; subtracting $1$ offsets the submitter's own vote; $T$ is the time elapsed since the entry was submitted, in hours; the +2 keeps the newest posts from making the denominator too small the choice of 2 may be because it takes an average of two hours for an original article to appear elsewhere and then be reposted to Hacker News ; $G$ is the gravity factor, which defaults to $1.8$ in the algorithm and determines how quickly a post's ranking falls, much like the idea of gravitational acceleration. This mechanism automatically filters out content the community agrees is valuable and not yet stale, keeping high-quality technical discussion, startup insights, and cutting-edge papers afloat. It is also basically comprehensive enough. I do not actually read much of it day to day, but I am sharing it here anyway. Current Affairs Then there is current affairs: The Bedtime News Editorial Department WeChat Account Updated every night. The Bedtime News Editorial Department account is the main business of Ma Dugong's studio. Although people on the internet have plenty of criticism for Ma Dugong, the news in the Bedtime News Editorial Department account is still in the higher tier of quality. Every item is distilled into a few key points; open it while you brush your teeth and you will have a basic grasp of what happened today. If your way of looking at problems leans toward “seeking truth from facts” and you dislike preset positions, then his Bilibili account Ma Dugong is worth following too. His analytical framework especially the long-form videos on Bilibili can also offer a lot of “counterintuitive” perspectives. Almost every episode sparks discussion on Zhihu, and when you have nothing else to do you can head over to Zhihu and see the different takes on a single event—which is quite nice, actually! Military Intelligence D7 This is one of the few current-affairs creators I follow who demands a lot of his sources and is not especially emotional no “win, win, win” 😭 . His presentations are very clearly structured, usually organized by region Iran, Russia-Ukraine, the Asia-Pacific, the United States to sort through recent developments. I have always loved surfing the internet and collecting all kinds of strange and wonderful websites and sources of information. Sharing them back and forth with classmates brought me plenty of new ones, and over time they became a shared language among us. My four years of university were, I would say, the four years in which I grew up the fastest socially: I went through a lot and saw a lot. Everything I want to share in this article is something I have been reading all along, and they are the sources I genuinely like. If you have any of your own you would like to share, please leave a comment below! 👏

Tech News

Ruan Yifeng's Web Log

https://www.ruanyifeng.com/blog/

Teacher Ruan's blog is probably the best known and most familiar of all Chinese personal blogs, and the “Technology Enthusiast Weekly” on this site has become a Friday ritual that many people (myself included) never miss.

It is not confined to pure technology; it reads more like a general-interest magazine for the digital age. It covers the author's observations and thoughts on technology, tech news, excellent articles, new tool recommendations, digests, interesting comments, and more. Add the cover image and introduction the author carefully picks each week, and the content is remarkably rich 🤩—enough to serve as a weekly roundup of tech highlights.

My favorite part is the author's tech observations, which are full of interesting thoughts and insights and often leave me feeling as though my cerebral cortex has been swapped out for a new one. Then there is the article recommendation section: I can honestly say that it is mainly through this weekly that I have come across many excellent personal bloggers and fresh ideas (the kind that set trends!).

Chaping's WeChat Account

Updated at midnight sharp every night, Chaping is more like a “tech midnight snack.” On the many nights I was busy fixing bugs 🥱, I would open it at midnight for a bit of diversion. It skims quickly through the day's important little tech news, mostly the stuff closely tied to us users. It also runs short analysis and discussion pieces on whatever topics are currently hot.

Chaping's main distinguishing feature is the way it explains hardcore tech news and business developments in very plain language laced with internet memes. The interactions in the comments are usually full of jokes too, and it even has a Daily Joke and an interactive section that gets discussions going in the comments, loosening the nerves wound tight by the day.

Hacker News

https://news.ycombinator.com/

This is a minimalist tech community run by Y Combinator, and an important window through which I get “raw information.” For me, what draws me in most is its ranking algorithm:

$$
Score = \frac{P - 1}{(T + 2)^G}
$$

where,

  • $P$ is the entry's score; subtracting $1$ offsets the submitter's own vote;
  • $T$ is the time elapsed since the entry was submitted, in hours; the +2 keeps the newest posts from making the denominator too small (the choice of 2 may be because it takes an average of two hours for an original article to appear elsewhere and then be reposted to Hacker News);
  • $G$ is the gravity factor, which defaults to $1.8$ in the algorithm and determines how quickly a post's ranking falls, much like the idea of gravitational acceleration.

This mechanism automatically filters out content the community agrees is valuable and not yet stale, keeping high-quality technical discussion, startup insights, and cutting-edge papers afloat. It is also basically comprehensive enough. I do not actually read much of it day to day, but I am sharing it here anyway.

Current Affairs

Then there is current affairs:

The Bedtime News Editorial Department WeChat Account

Updated every night. The Bedtime News Editorial Department account is the main business of Ma Dugong's studio. Although people on the internet have plenty of criticism for Ma Dugong, the news in the Bedtime News Editorial Department account is still in the higher tier of quality. Every item is distilled into a few key points; open it while you brush your teeth and you will have a basic grasp of what happened today.

If your way of looking at problems leans toward “seeking truth from facts” and you dislike preset positions, then his Bilibili account Ma Dugong is worth following too. His analytical framework (especially the long-form videos on Bilibili) can also offer a lot of “counterintuitive” perspectives. Almost every episode sparks discussion on Zhihu, and when you have nothing else to do you can head over to Zhihu and see the different takes on a single event—which is quite nice, actually!

https://space.bilibili.com/448165099

His presentations are very clearly structured, usually organized by region (Iran, Russia-Ukraine, the Asia-Pacific, the United States) to sort through recent developments. When things were busy he posted almost daily; the frequency has slowed recently, but the content still keeps up high information density and objectivity, avoiding the inflammatory language common to military content—which suits my taste rather well.

There are, in fact, a great many sources that lean toward specific technologies. This is the “source” of many frontier technologies—the earliest explanations of foundational work such as Transformer and BERT came from here. It mainly publishes the latest progress in machine learning, natural language processing, computer vision, and quantum computing (all very cool technologies 😯!). Some of it is on the research-heavy side, but through its accessible posts you can directly feel the direction in which “future technology” is evolving, and seeing them, you are bound to feel at least a little excited.

items.content_html:
For exploration and fun, my old terminal had been stuffed with oh-my-zsh and all kinds of plugins. At some point I could no longer remember what I had installed. Worse, the interface looked so awkward that I did not even want to open it.

Recently I saw Ghostty on Bilibili, along with a few terminal customization videos that looked surprisingly nice. So this time I decided to start from zero and rebuild my terminal properly.

I started using the terminal shortly after I bought my Mac and finished setting up the development environment. Back then I knew almost nothing about customization tools like Raycast or Bartender, let alone the command line habits that macOS users often build over time.

Later, my older cousin tried to teach me a few things. When he opened my computer, he exclaimed: "Why is your computer so primitive?"

That was probably the first time I realized how different macOS habits could be from Windows habits. I have always preferred simple setups on Windows too, but from that moment on I started exploring how to make my Mac environment both prettier and more useful.

A Messy Beginning

For a long time, my terminal looked close to the default style. I forgot to keep screenshots, but it was basically a gray background with plain text. Following different online tutorials, I installed iTerm2, oh-my-zsh, and a large number of other plugins.

The problem was that the whole setup became too messy. I either forgot how to use some plugins, or simply never used them at all. The terminal still worked, but it often required plugin updates, and opening a new terminal window had more than a second of delay. That became annoying.

So I decided to rebuild everything and write down the process. It may also serve as a reference for classmates who recently bought a Mac and want a clean terminal setup.

Sharpen the Tools First

Choosing the right tools is the core of this rebuild. My criteria were simple:

  1. Performance first: short startup time and fast rendering.
  2. Low maintenance cost: usable out of the box, easy to customize, clear configuration path, and not dependent on plugin stacking.
  3. Good looking: good looks are productivity. :)

In the end, I chose this combination: Ghostty + native Zsh + Starship + Yazi. It covers my current needs almost completely, and I can add smaller tools later if needed.

After such a long time, I realized I barely used most of the old oh-my-zsh plugins. Installing oh-my-zsh again does not make much sense for me right now. This article also shares a similar idea: A Guide to the Zsh Line Editor with Examples.

Let me briefly introduce the tools.

Ghostty: Terminal Emulator

The official docs describe it like this:

Ghostty is a fast, feature-rich, and cross-platform terminal emulator that uses platform-native UI and GPU acceleration.

Similar tools include Terminal.app, iTerm2, Warp, WezTerm, Alacritty, Kitty, and more.

Why did I choose Ghostty among so many options? I first noticed it because Boris Cherny recommended it. I tried it and unexpectedly found that it fit me very well.

  • It is compiled from Zig to native machine code, avoiding VM/interpreter overhead and GC pauses.
  • Its character buffer maps directly to GPU memory, skipping CPU round trips.
  • It parses TOML configuration once at startup and does not rely on plugin hot reload, which makes it fast. The configuration is also centralized in one TOML file, so settings are clear and easy to understand.

After using it for a while, Ghostty starts much faster than my previous setup, and memory usage is reasonable. It feels close to what I imagine a modern terminal should be.

Starship: Prompt Engine

Similar tool: oh-my-posh.

Starship is written in Rust and distributed as a compiled program. It starts very quickly. As a prompt engine, it replaces the main use case I previously relied on oh-my-zsh for: making the prompt look nice.

The old setup had to run a pile of shell scripts every time the terminal opened. Now startup is faster, and the whole experience feels much smoother.

Yazi: Async File Manager

Yazi is somewhat like macOS Finder, but controlled through the keyboard. Once you understand your machine's file structure, it feels more efficient than constantly typing cd and ls.

It is also written in Rust, so loading is fast. It supports live previews, which means you do not have to find a file and press Space just to inspect it. It can preview text, images, and many other files directly.

It also uses Vim-style keybindings. If you have used Vim before, it feels natural. Even if you have not, you can probably learn the basics quickly, and the ? help menu is friendly.

Reproducible Setup Steps

Prerequisites

Install Homebrew, the command-line package manager for macOS, and a Nerd Font for terminal icons.

Install Homebrew:

/bin/bash -c "$(curl -fsSL https://raw.githubusercontent.com/Homebrew/install/HEAD/install.sh)"

Update Homebrew:

brew update

Install the Software

# Font
brew install --cask font-jetbrains-mono-nerd-font

# Terminal emulator
brew install --cask ghostty

# Prompt engine
brew install starship

# File manager + preview dependencies
brew install yazi ffmpegthumbnailer sevenzip poppler jq fd ripgrep fzf

# Other useful tools
# Command autosuggestions + syntax highlighting
brew install zsh-autosuggestions zsh-syntax-highlighting

Configure Ghostty

Open Ghostty and press Command + ,. A TOML config file should appear. You can copy my config into it:

# ===== Font settings =====
font-family = JetBrainsMono Nerd Font
font-size = 14

# ===== Window padding =====
window-padding-x = 12
window-padding-y = 12

# ===== Cursor and scrolling =====
cursor-style = block
scrollback-limit = 10000
copy-on-select = true

# ===== Theme =====
theme = Catppuccin Mocha

# ===== Quick terminal: Cmd + backtick =====
keybind = cmd+`=toggle_quick_terminal

At this point, the terminal should already look much better.

Next is Starship. You can also read the official Starship configuration docs.

Create the config file:

mkdir -p ~/.config && touch ~/.config/starship.toml

Open it:

nano ~/.config/starship.toml

If you are not familiar with nano or Vim, you can use VS Code and open the file with code ~/.config/starship.toml.

My config:

"$schema" = 'https://starship.rs/config-schema.json'

format = """
[](red)\
$os\
$username\
[](bg:peach fg:red)\
$directory\
[](bg:yellow fg:peach)\
$git_branch\
$git_status\
[](fg:yellow bg:green)\
$c\
$rust\
$golang\
$nodejs\
$php\
$java\
$kotlin\
$haskell\
$python\
[](fg:green bg:sapphire)\
$conda\
[](fg:sapphire bg:lavender)\
$time\
[ ](fg:lavender)\
$cmd_duration\
$line_break\
$character"""

palette = 'catppuccin_mocha'

[os]
disabled = false
style = "bg:red fg:crust"

[os.symbols]
Windows = ""
Ubuntu = "󰕈"
SUSE = ""
Raspbian = "󰐿"
Mint = "󰣭"
Macos = "󰀵"
Manjaro = ""
Linux = "󰌽"

Amazon = ""
Android = ""
AOSC = ""
Arch = "󰣇"
Artix = "󰣇"
CentOS = ""
Debian = "󰣚"
Redhat = "󱄛"
RedHatEnterprise = "󱄛"

[username]
show_always = true
style_user = "bg:red fg:crust"

format = '[ $user]($style)'

[directory]
style = "bg:peach fg:crust"
format = "[ $path ]($style)"
truncation_length = 3
truncation_symbol = "…/"

[directory.substitutions]
"Documents" = "󰈙 "
"Downloads" = " "
"Music" = "󰝚 "
"Pictures" = " "
"Developer" = "󰲋 "

[git_branch]
symbol = ""
style = "bg:yellow"
format = '[[ $symbol $branch ](fg:crust bg:yellow)]($style)'

[git_status]
style = "bg:yellow"
format = '[[($all_status$ahead_behind )](fg:crust bg:yellow)]($style)'

[nodejs]
symbol = ""
style = "bg:green"
format = '[[ $symbol( $version) ](fg:crust bg:green)]($style)'

[c]
symbol = " "
style = "bg:green"

[rust]
symbol = ""
style = "bg:green"
format = '[[ $symbol( $version) ](fg:crust bg:green)]($style)'

[golang]
symbol = ""
style = "bg:green"
format = '[[ $symbol( $version) ](fg:crust bg:green)]($style)'

[php]
symbol = ""
style = "bg:green"
format = '[[ $symbol( $version) ](fg:crust bg:green)]($style)'

[java]
symbol = " "
style = "bg:green"
format = '[[ $symbol( $version) ](fg:crust bg:green)]($style)'

[kotlin]
symbol = ""

[python]

format = '[[ $symbol( $version)(\(#$virtualenv\)) ](fg:crust bg:green)]($style)'

[docker_context]
symbol = ""
style = "bg:sapphire"
format = '[[ $symbol( $context) ](fg:crust bg:sapphire)]($style)'

[conda]
symbol = "  "
style = "fg:crust bg:sapphire"
format = '[$symbol$environment ]($style)'
ignore_base = false

[time]
disabled = false
time_format = "%R"
style = "bg:lavender"
format = '[[  $time ](fg:crust bg:lavender)]($style)'

[line_break]
disabled = true

[character]
disabled = false
success_symbol = '[❯](bold fg:green)'
error_symbol = '[❯](bold fg:red)'
vimcmd_symbol = '[❮](bold fg:green)'
vimcmd_replace_one_symbol = '[❮](bold fg:lavender)'
vimcmd_replace_symbol = '[❮](bold fg:lavender)'
vimcmd_visual_symbol = '[❮](bold fg:yellow)'

[cmd_duration]
show_milliseconds = true
format = " in $duration "
style = "bg:lavender"
disabled = false
show_notifications = true
min_time_to_notify = 45000

[palettes.catppuccin_mocha]
rosewater = "#f5e0dc"
flamingo = "#f2cdcd"
pink = "#f5c2e7"
mauve = "#cba6f7"
red = "#f38ba8"
maroon = "#eba0ac"
peach = "#fab387"
yellow = "#f9e2af"
green = "#a6e3a1"
teal = "#94e2d5"
sky = "#89dceb"
sapphire = "#74c7ec"
blue = "#89b4fa"
lavender = "#b4befe"
text = "#cdd6f4"
subtext1 = "#bac2de"
subtext0 = "#a6adc8"
overlay2 = "#9399b2"
overlay1 = "#7f849c"
overlay0 = "#6c7086"
surface2 = "#585b70"
surface1 = "#45475a"
surface0 = "#313244"
base = "#1e1e2e"
mantle = "#181825"
crust = "#11111b"

If you want another theme, list Starship presets with:

starship preset --list

It will show options such as bracketed-segments, catppuccin-powerline, tokyo-night, and more.

Apply a preset like this:

starship preset tokyo-night > ~/.config/starship.toml

Finally, configure Zsh. I recommend appending the following to your existing ~/.zshrc instead of overwriting it, because your file may already contain Conda, Node, or other environment settings.

nano ~/.zshrc

# ===== Homebrew: macOS package manager =====
export PATH="/opt/homebrew/bin:$PATH"

# ===== Starship =====
eval "$(starship init zsh)"

# ===== Completion =====
autoload -Uz compinit && compinit

# ===== Yazi terminal file manager =====
function y() {
  local tmp="$(mktemp -t "yazi-cwd.XXXXXX")" cwd
  yazi "$@" --cwd-file="$tmp"
  if cwd="$(command cat -- "$tmp")" && [ -n "$cwd" ] && [ "$cwd" != "$PWD" ]; then
    builtin cd -- "$cwd"
  fi
  rm -f -- "$tmp"
}

# yy as a shortcut for yazi
alias yy="y"

# ===== Zsh Autosuggestions =====
source /opt/homebrew/share/zsh-autosuggestions/zsh-autosuggestions.zsh

# ===== Zsh Syntax Highlighting =====
source /opt/homebrew/share/zsh-syntax-highlighting/zsh-syntax-highlighting.zsh

Verify the Setup

exec zsh

If You Use VS Code

If you use VS Code or another editor and see strange characters in the integrated terminal, the problem is usually the font. Open settings, search for terminal font, and set it to:

JetBrainsMono Nerd Font

Now you should have a beautiful and practical terminal.

Why This Is Worth the Time

The terminal is not just a tool. For developers, it is one of the workbenches we face every day. With vibe coding becoming more common, terminal usage is also becoming more frequent. A well-configured terminal can make the whole workflow feel clearer and more pleasant.

  • Ghostty: Official Site | GitHub
  • Starship: Official Site | GitHub
  • Yazi: Official Site | GitHub

This setup was verified with:

  • Ghostty 1.3.1 (stable)
  • Starship 1.24.2
  • Yazi 0.3.0

Configuration syntax may differ across versions. If you run into problems, check the official docs for your installed version first.

items.title: When Open Source Is Only a Prompt: I Found a Ridiculous New Way to Open Source
items.content_text: Recently, while wandering around GitHub, I came across a project that felt both shocking and funny: voice-input-src . It is a voice input tool built for Mac. When you opened the repository, you will not find any traditional Swift source code. items.content_html:
Recently, while wandering around GitHub, I came across a project that felt both shocking and funny: voice-input-src. It is a voice input tool built for Mac.

When you opened the repository, you will not find any traditional Swift source code. Instead, the repo contains only an extremely detailed prompt written for AI, specifically Claude, with both Chinese and English instructions.

That made me curious: Can this kind of open source actually work? Can users really reproduce a usable app from this? Since I happen to have a MacBook, I decided to try reproducing it on my own machine and see whether this open-source model was feasible.

Project Breakdown: Is This Really "Source Code"?

1. An Extremely Minimal Repository

The project has a README.md file containing the required prompt text, and nothing else.

I have to admit, this kind of open-source project is very easy to understand.

2. Prompt as Source Code

Traditional open source is "humans read code, compilers execute code." This project is more like "humans read the prompt, AI executes the prompt."

The author, yetone, even created a separate voice-input-dist repository to store the app source code generated by AI. This cleanly separates the "source" from the "artifact," and it also makes comparison easier for users.

It is a small but interesting design choice.

What Is Hidden Inside the Prompt?

Since the prompt is basically the only thing we can inspect in this repository, I analyzed it before trying to reproduce the project.

This is not a casual requirement document written by someone who knows nothing about programming. It is a document written by someone who clearly understands macOS APIs and implementation details.

Module Implementation Details
Speech Recognition Uses Apple's Speech Recognition framework, supports streaming transcription, defaults to Chinese.
Global Hotkey Listens to the Fn key through global event monitoring with CGEvent tap, while suppressing the default behavior to prevent the emoji panel from opening.
Floating UI Borderless NSPanel, visual blur effects, and real-time waveform animation driven by audio RMS rather than fake animation.
Input Method Compatibility Detects the current input method, switches to the ABC keyboard before pasting to avoid Cmd+V interception, then restores the original input method.
LLM Post-processing Calls an OpenAI-compatible API for correction, only fixing obvious mistakes such as "配森" -> "Python".

From these details, it is clear that the author knew exactly which frameworks to call, which components to use, what conflicts might appear later, and how those conflicts should be handled.

Because the author understands the technical background and implementation difficulties well enough, he could write such a precise project-level prompt. One GitHub issue even commented:

This thing is the real prompt development tutorial.

My Reproduction Attempt on My Mac

To verify whether this kind of open source is actually effective, and also to experience this slightly wild form of prompt engineering, I ran a complete "from prompt to app" experiment on my Mac.

1. Environment

  • Mac: My 2021 M1 Pro MacBook, running Tahoe 26.3.1.
  • AI tool: Codex, using GPT 5.4 Extra High. I wanted to see whether a model different from the author's Claude setup could still succeed.

Here is my device configuration:

2. Steps

  1. Feed the prompt: Send the full prompt from the repository to Codex.
  2. Functional acceptance testing: Definitely not because I do not know Swift well enough to read all the generated code.

Checklist:

✅ Can the Fn key reliably start recording without opening the emoji panel?
✅ Does the floating waveform change in real time with volume?
✅ How accurate is Chinese recognition? Does LLM correction work?

3. Actual Implementation

On my machine, the app did not build successfully on the first attempt. The first full build took about 23 minutes and cost $1.3994 USD. After that, two small runtime/build issues appeared, so I asked Codex to fix them twice. Including fixes, the total cost was $1.9734 USD.

Here is Codex's summary of the two fixes:

These two fixes essentially solved one compile-time problem and one runtime crash.

The first fix was in PasteboardInjector.swift line 18. The original code used an expression like pasteboard.pasteboardItems?.map { ... } ?? [], relying on Swift to infer the type of items. In some cases, this optional chain plus empty-array fallback made type inference unstable, eventually causing an error at return PasteboardBackup(items: items). The fix was simple: explicitly write items as [Item]. This did not change any business logic; it only replaced "let the compiler guess" with "tell the compiler the type directly."

The second fix was in FloatingPanelController.swift line 93. The original code set collectionBehavior = [.canJoinAllSpaces, .fullScreenAuxiliary, .moveToActiveSpace, .ignoresCycle]. The issue is that .canJoinAllSpaces and .moveToActiveSpace conflict semantically. One means "join all Spaces," while the other means "move with the currently active Space." AppKit is sensitive to this kind of window behavior combination, and it can trigger an assertion that ends as an abort signal crash. The fix changed it to a more stable combination: keep .moveToActiveSpace, .fullScreenAuxiliary, and .ignoresCycle, add .transient, and remove .canJoinAllSpaces. The floating window can still appear in the current Space and alongside full-screen apps, but it no longer crashes during initialization.

Result

You can probably guess it: this entire article was dictated using the generated app.

The effect is actually pretty good. Characters appear quickly, faster and more immediate than Apple's built-in dictation, and invoking it is more convenient.

Here is what it looked like:

As for shortcomings, you can see that the text was not centered nicely at first, which felt a bit uncomfortable. I later prompted Codex to fix that too. Overall, my version still did not look as polished as the author's Claude-generated demo, but at least it worked.

Is This the Future of Open Source, or Just a Joke?

1. The Positive View: Extreme DRY

  • Very low maintenance cost: The author does not need to care about Xcode version changes or Swift syntax evolution. He only provides a requirements document.
  • Reproducibility: As long as the AI model is capable enough, anyone can generate a functionally similar app at any time.
  • Easy sharing: This way of sharing is direct. Compared with publishing a huge codebase vibe-coded from scratch, a carefully written prompt may actually be cleaner in some cases.

2. The Slightly Negative View

  • Uncontrollability: Generated code quality depends heavily on the AI model. It is hard to guarantee identical results every time. My Codex version was usable, but visually not as good as the author's demo.
  • Operational friction: To generate the code, users still need an AI environment and enough budget. For small projects this is fine, but larger projects can become expensive. Users also have to wait for generation, which is less convenient than downloading a release from the author.

Overall, I do not think this experiment is a bad thing. On the contrary, the author's creative repo structure gave me a small shock.

Maybe this should be understood less as a concrete project distribution method and more as an excellent AI tutorial. To write a prompt like the author's, you still need solid technical knowledge and a clear understanding of the target platform.

At least for me, I definitely could not write such a perfect prompt in one shot.

If you have some spare time, I recommend trying it yourself.

items.title: My First Blog
items.content_text: My website has been online for nearly 30 days, and only now do I have this first blog post in the true sense. I actually wanted to wait until the website in my initial plan was mostly finished before I started writing. It is also a way to record the beginning and journey of this little site. So, let's begin. Why did I build this website? When it comes to personal websites, or personal blogs, I have been exposed to the concept since childhood. Many books I read were essentially collections of personal online blog posts and essays. One example I really liked was 万万没想到 by Weigang Wan, which was compiled from his online journals. I used to think writing blogs was something really cool, but never have I imagined that one day I would also want to write and keep track of my own life. The shift from reading others' blogs to writing my own was actually accidental. One day I was scrolling 知乎 and saw a question: "What should you do while you're still young?" It was the typical kind of question for asking advice for young people. I read several answers and one of them still sticks with me to this day. Its core idea was: "While you're young, leave yourself more beautiful memories. Even when life gets hard later, at least those memories can hold you up." That feels true. When I look back at the childhood photos my parents took for me, I still feel warm inside. I don't actually remember much from those years, but by watching old videos with my parents time and time again, and hearing them tell those stories time and time again, made even memories that never truly should be existed in my mind become vivid. Maybe that's why many classmates are surprised I can remember things from so long ago. During my university years, I also went through a vast transition: from a life of fixed study-and-exam routines primary school to high school , to arranging my own time and life. I joined many team-based competitions and made many choices that did not follow the mainstream. There were months when I stayed up all night every day just studying. There were also carefree days when I could just pack up and travel on impulse. I met friends and classmates from different cities and different age groups in society. I also changed from someone who ignored what was happening outside, to someone who started paying attention to social issues and current events. After all this, it was hard not to want to document my life and transformation. Ideas stop at imagination; execution depends on things actually happening. During my 考研 preparation period, I came across a personal website with many friend links. I started visiting different interesting personal sites. Many of them were from Chinese college students recording their study notes and daily life. They were not all "guru-level" blogs full of big insights though some certainly were . But still, through those ordinary records, I felt like I had met new friends with people I never met in person. Combined with the thoughts I had already been carrying, this finally pushed me to decide to build my own site. So after the exam, I began the journey. How was the website built? As everyone knows, websites are essentially frontend work. AI is already very strong in this area. It not only makes building easier, but can also produce interfaces with good interaction and visual quality. If someone still insists on purely old-school programming and types everything from scratch today, it's hard to say whether people would admire it or laugh at it. At the same time, there are many open-source blog templates for example, there are lots of beautiful templates on Hexo . If you directly use one, you can avoid reinventing the wheel. It's fast and practical, and often prettier than a hand-drawn draft made by one person. So from the early stage, when I was building this site, I kept thinking about what's convenient, especially how to make AI convenient to use. Across the whole internet frontend ecosystem, React has the largest share. That also means AI has seen the most React-related code, which makes future AI-assisted modifications easier. Also, when I was a sophomore, my older cousin asked me to learn some React, but I never got real practice. I always wanted to try it properly. Overall, React really suited me well: someone who wanted to build from scratch, experience the full React development process, and create a website with personal ideas. Image source: eleopardsolutions So I chose as the core stack of my website. After I finished the overall framework and structure myself, it was time for AI to shine. As the site improved bit by bit and animations were adjusted continuously, the look I had in mind gradually became real you can see more details on our Timeline page . Later, with free hosting and image services from Vercel and Cloudflare, our website finally went live, and in a cost-effective way. There are already lots of tutorials online for the exact process, so I won't repeat them here. What's next？ I am already quite satisfied with this little site, but the content is still very empty. Right now it mostly has a shell. So moving forward, I will document my life, especially my university life. If someone reads this before entering college, maybe they can learn from my mistakes in advance, and maybe pick up a bit of useful experience from me too. Haha. To expand this site, I will also keep working in my spare time on two additional projects. Maybe I can make a project collection page? Or perhaps share some great papers and blog posts I have read. Who knows? Just let everything happen!

Maybe that's why many classmates are surprised I can remember things from so long ago.

During my university years, I also went through a vast transition: from a life of fixed study-and-exam routines (primary school to high school), to arranging my own time and life. I joined many team-based competitions and made many choices that did not follow the mainstream. There were months when I stayed up all night every day just studying. There were also carefree days when I could just pack up and travel on impulse.

I met friends and classmates from different cities and different age groups in society. I also changed from someone who ignored what was happening outside, to someone who started paying attention to social issues and current events.

After all this, it was hard not to want to document my life and transformation.

Ideas stop at imagination; execution depends on things actually happening.

During my 考研 preparation period, I came across a personal website with many friend links. I started visiting different interesting personal sites. Many of them were from Chinese college students recording their study notes and daily life. They were not all "guru-level" blogs full of big insights (though some certainly were). But still, through those ordinary records, I felt like I had met new friends with people I never met in person.

Combined with the thoughts I had already been carrying, this finally pushed me to decide to build my own site. So after the exam, I began the journey.

How was the website built?

As everyone knows, websites are essentially frontend work. AI is already very strong in this area. It not only makes building easier, but can also produce interfaces with good interaction and visual quality.

If someone still insists on purely old-school programming and types everything from scratch today, it's hard to say whether people would admire it or laugh at it.

At the same time, there are many open-source blog templates (for example, there are lots of beautiful templates on Hexo). If you directly use one, you can avoid reinventing the wheel. It's fast and practical, and often prettier than a hand-drawn draft made by one person.

So from the early stage, when I was building this site, I kept thinking about what's convenient, especially how to make AI convenient to use. Image source: eleopardsolutions

So I chose React + Vite + Tailwind CSS as the core stack of my website. After I finished the overall framework and structure myself, it was time for AI to shine.

As the site improved bit by bit and animations were adjusted continuously, the look I had in mind gradually became real (you can see more details on our Timeline page). Later, with free hosting and image services from Vercel and Cloudflare, our website finally went live, and in a cost-effective way. (There are already lots of tutorials online for the exact process, so I won't repeat them here.)

What's next？

I am already quite satisfied with this little site, but the content is still very empty. Right now it mostly has a shell. So moving forward, I will document my life, especially my university life.

If someone reads this before entering college, maybe they can learn from my mistakes in advance, and maybe pick up a bit of useful experience from me too. Haha.

To expand this site, I will also keep working in my spare time on two additional projects. Maybe I can make a project collection page? Or perhaps share some great papers and blog posts I have read.

Who knows? Just let everything happen!

items.title: Guangzhou Travel Notes
items.content_text: Itinerary: 3/22: Train at 8:50 AM - Arrive in Guangzhou at 12:30 PM - Dim sum at Dian Du De - Chen Clan Ancestral Hall - Liwan Lake - Yongqing Fang - Shangxiajiu - Shamian Island - Canton Customs - Sacred Heart Cathedral - Beijing Road - Guesthouse - Dafo Temple 3/23: Early morning meetup with a new friend at Sun Yat-sen Memorial Hall - Walk to Nanyue King Museum - Bamboo-pressed noodles - Yuexiu Park - Dongshankou - Taikoo Hui - Gym - Saizeriya - Huacheng Square - Canton Tower - Haixinsha - Guesthouse 3/24: Guangzhou Museum of Art - Sun Yat-sen University - APM Line - Xihua Road - Train station Last Friday, our database teacher took a day off, which unexpectedly gave us free time and turned into a three-day mini holiday. Taking this chance, my close buddy and I planned a trip to Guangzhou, and we also wanted to meet his childhood friend there. So we set off early on Friday morning. My ticket was to Guangzhou East Station. Normally, stations named "East" or "West" are newer and larger. But this one felt the opposite. Guangzhou must have developed so early that even the later-built stations already feel old. The moment we walked out, we were in a bustling district: shiny commercial streets mixed with aging residential blocks, with a few thick, old, lively trees on both sides of the road casting shade over the wide sidewalks. We gradually tuned into the rhythm of the city. It took us a while, but eventually we caught it: long history, rich daily life, youth, and vitality. We quickly decided to go for morning tea. My buddy asked several classmates, and they all recommended Dian Du De. It was a little pricey, but the quality and service were excellent. We went to the branch closest to the station there were a few izakayas across the street; stepping in felt like entering a Japanese drama, totally different from the lively Chinese street outside , and started feasting. The two of us spent 250 RMB and basically tried a whole range of dishes. After the meal we took an elevator, then realized it only went up. Buttons from floors 4 to 11 were all lit and couldn't be canceled. So my friend and I, together with an elderly man, just kept riding floor by floor and eventually came back down to the ground from what had originally been the second floor. The old man chatted in Cantonese, different from what you hear in Hong Kong movies, and complained about a lot of things. I only clearly understood one phrase: "damn it." Just like Lu Xun wrote, that phrase is nationally unified. After that we quickly checked off all the recommended spots from Xiaohongshu. During the process, we slowly resonated with Guangzhou itself: we watched elderly bands playing in riverside parks along the Pearl River, seniors doing partner dancing, little opera stages in parks, filmed with foreign friends, saw young influencers posing at check-in spots, watched young office workers hurrying by, middle-aged people exercising steadily, elementary school kids choosing ice cream after class, parents picking up children after work, and children still playing before their parents arrived. Day one ended quickly. We were exhausted and looked forward to deep sleep that night. Three-Person Walkabout Early on the second day, we skipped refined breakfast shops and went to a roadside stand at a quiet crossroads. We had rice noodles for 5 RMB, and they were surprisingly great 🎉. We met my buddy's childhood friend at Sun Yat-sen Memorial Hall. At first we were not familiar, just acquainted, and didn't talk much. After visiting the memorial hall together, we passed a Taoist temple on our way to the Nanyue King Museum. Somewhere along that walk, the awkwardness faded and our conversation gradually opened up. After the Nanyue King Museum, we went to a noodle shop that our friend's childhood friend said was good. Unexpectedly, the bamboo-pressed noodles were made with fish-bone broth. I didn't eat a single bite I don't like seafood 😟 , and we continued on. After wandering for a long time, none of us knew what to do next, so I suggested going to the gym our friend's childhood friend is incredibly fit! . We found a cheap gym, but it required reservation and wouldn't let us train on the spot. So we switched to a better one. The service was excellent, and the equipment was new and great. I learned a lot from him. I updated my training plan, clarified my training goals, learned many new movements and details, and also checked whether my existing form was standard. I benefited a lot. Then we went to Canton Tower. Another day ended in complete exhaustion. Train Delay We got up early and walked again to the Guangzhou Museum of Art, because we had forgotten to reserve Guangdong Provincial Museum and couldn't get in. After a quick visit, we arrived at the gate of Sun Yat-sen University. I had already contacted another close friend studying there. He told us about a side gate where we could enter directly without prior reservation since we failed to reserve in advance . He also kindly told us which places on campus were worth visiting. Seeing him study in such a beautiful place made me really envious. I started imagining that one day I could study there too. Then we took a taxi to the APM line, where we heard we could see flowers, but the queue was too long. So we refunded and switched to a snack street. We tried many new foods there. One snack called bo bo gui looked like rice cake with brown sugar syrup, but it turned out to be garlic oil. It left a bad smell in our mouths and was salty, not very tasty. After eating, we rushed to the train station, expecting to arrive on time according to plan, but ran into unexpected traffic and delays. We even cut into line at the station and sprinted all the way to the gate, but were still stopped. If we had arrived just five minutes earlier, we could have made it such a pity . Then came ticket changes. My buddy couldn't get a refund after the train departure and lost 388 RMB. I paid over 110 RMB in service fees to change mine. We didn't get back to Xiamen until 10 PM. Overall, those three days were full and joyful, with rich experiences, both ups and downs. This season is actually a great time to visit Guangzhou. The sun is strong, but it's not unbearably hot. We walked so much that we were completely worn out, averaging 38,000 steps per day. I sincerely hope that one day I can study in Guangzhou, or even stay there for a while and truly live there.

Day one ended quickly. We were exhausted and looked forward to deep sleep that night.

Three-Person Walkabout

Early on the second day, we skipped refined breakfast shops and went to a roadside stand at a quiet crossroads. We had rice noodles for 5 RMB, and they were surprisingly great 🎉. We met my buddy's childhood friend at Sun Yat-sen Memorial Hall. At first we were not familiar, just acquainted, and didn't talk much. After visiting the memorial hall together, we passed a Taoist temple on our way to the Nanyue King Museum. Somewhere along that walk, the awkwardness faded and our conversation gradually opened up.

After the Nanyue King Museum, we went to a noodle shop that our friend's childhood friend said was good. Unexpectedly, the bamboo-pressed noodles were made with fish-bone broth. I didn't eat a single bite (I don't like seafood 😟), and we continued on.

After wandering for a long time, none of us knew what to do next, so I suggested going to the gym (our friend's childhood friend is incredibly fit!). We found a cheap gym, but it required reservation and wouldn't let us train on the spot. So we switched to a better one. The service was excellent, and the equipment was new and great. I learned a lot from him. I updated my training plan, clarified my training goals, learned many new movements and details, and also checked whether my existing form was standard. I benefited a lot.

Then we went to Canton Tower. Another day ended in complete exhaustion.

Train Delay

We got up early and walked again to the Guangzhou Museum of Art, because we had forgotten to reserve Guangdong Provincial Museum and couldn't get in. After a quick visit, we arrived at the gate of Sun Yat-sen University.

I had already contacted another close friend studying there. He told us about a side gate where we could enter directly without prior reservation (since we failed to reserve in advance). He also kindly told us which places on campus were worth visiting. Seeing him study in such a beautiful place made me really envious. I started imagining that one day I could study there too.

Then we took a taxi to the APM line, where we heard we could see flowers, but the queue was too long. So we refunded and switched to a snack street. We tried many new foods there. One snack called bo bo gui looked like rice cake with brown sugar syrup, but it turned out to be garlic oil. It left a bad smell in our mouths and was salty, not very tasty.

After eating, we rushed to the train station, expecting to arrive on time according to plan, but ran into unexpected traffic and delays. We even cut into line at the station and sprinted all the way to the gate, but were still stopped. If we had arrived just five minutes earlier, we could have made it (such a pity).

Then came ticket changes. My buddy couldn't get a refund after the train departure and lost 388 RMB. I paid over 110 RMB in service fees to change mine. We didn't get back to Xiamen until 10 PM.

Overall, those three days were full and joyful, with rich experiences, both ups and downs. This season is actually a great time to visit Guangzhou. The sun is strong, but it's not unbearably hot. We walked so much that we were completely worn out, averaging 38,000 steps per day. I sincerely hope that one day I can study in Guangzhou, or even stay there for a while and truly live there.

items.title: Notes from Xi'an
items.content_text: AI translation notice: This English version was translated from the original Chinese article with AI assistance. Some nuances may differ from the original. October 27: Wake up at 4:30 a.m. and go to the airport → arrive in Xi'an at 9:50 → first lunch stop Cantonese beef hot pot → Terracotta Warriors Museum → Bell Tower → Muslim Quarter → Drum Tower → Bell Tower → homestay October 28: Wake up at 6:50 a.m. → buy medicine → meet Le-ge → walk on the city wall → Beilin Museum → Shaanxi History Museum → homestay → Giant Wild Goose Pagoda → Great Tang All Day Mall → homestay October 29: Wake up at 7:00 a.m. → Small Wild Goose Pagoda → airport An Exciting Day — October 27 Our flight left at 6:50 in the morning, so I needed to get up around 4:30 and go to bed early. I lay down at 11:30 but did not fall asleep until around one. All night I kept thinking that the next morning I would finally feel the autumn air of a place that felt like home. I was incredibly excited. When it was time to get up, I was surprisingly not tired at all. I set off for Xi'an full of energy. After arriving in Xi'an, we took the metro and followed our plan toward the Terracotta Warriors. We stopped to eat along the way because a restaurant's flyer looked interesting. The food was fine, but coming all the way to Xi'an to eat Cantonese food made the Guangdong member of our group feel personally defeated. Xi'an is very good at tourism. The metro stations had notes explaining which public-transport route to take to famous attractions, as well as how much a taxi should cost and how long it should take. This helps prevent visitors from being overcharged by unscrupulous drivers. I was genuinely moved by the effort this city had made to think about its visitors. We then reached the Terracotta Warriors . There was a little disappointment: two of the three people in our group decided not to hire a guide, so we went without one. After quickly walking through the three pits, we ran out of time and missed the Mausoleum of Qin Shi Huang. We also did not make it to Huaqing Palace, which is supposedly not that impressive anyway. Dinner that night was quite good. The restaurant was neither famous nor conspicuous, but according to the owner of the osmanthus-cake shop, it was authentic. When we asked for “Lao Liu's Lamb Paomo,” the shopkeeper's eyes lit up as she happily explained how to get there. Perhaps it really was good. The Wind on the City Wall — October 28 I woke up with irritated eyes because the homestay was not very clean, so I activated the Sharingan first thing in the morning. I went out to buy medicine and wasted more than ¥80. From now on, I will always bring some common medicines when traveling. After meeting Le-ge, we bought an egg-stuffed flatbread from a street stall. Eating a simple, ordinary, piping-hot breakfast in the slightly chilly autumn air felt like a small piece of human happiness. It was even more satisfying than eating a full meal in the warm cafeteria at my university in Xiamen. There were not many people on the northern section of the city wall, so we rode bicycles. The air was not very humid and felt much lighter, almost as though I did not need to inhale because it would flow into my lungs by itself and fill me up. My body seemed lighter too, as if buoyed by water. From the wall, the entire layout of Xi'an unfolded in the distance. The feeling of having one's expectations fulfilled was wonderful. The autumn wind refreshed me and blew away my stress; for a young person, perhaps this wind could not yet carry melancholy. Watching the kindergarten children running a “marathon” along the wall made the whole scene feel even more energetic. The Shaanxi History Museum was also completely without a guide. It was crowded, the space was relatively small, and the stuffy air made it difficult to settle down and appreciate the exhibits. The artifacts were all national treasures, and the guides seemed professional, but after one pass I did not retain a particularly deep impression. It was hard not to compare the museum with those I had visited before, especially since it is already such a remarkable institution. It might be more exciting if museums could exchange artifacts with other countries, allowing visitors to see the histories of different regions from the same period side by side. The British Museum offers something like that. As for the building itself, it is also hard to compare with the National Museum of China: one is narrow and crowded, the other grand and spacious. Despite these shortcomings, the Shaanxi History Museum left a strong impression on me. I hope I can return someday and listen to a proper guided tour. The Giant Wild Goose Pagoda and the Great Tang All Day Mall at night were genuinely awe-inspiring. The street design showed a lot of thought and encouraged visitors to interact with it: piano-key paving stones, dance-floor-style tiles that changed color, and fountains whose flow was controlled by the sound of the crowd. There were many performances along the street, including a viral “Mimou” show and a concert. The street was broad enough that even with imposing historical sculptures in the middle, snack stalls on both sides, and girls in Tang-style clothing taking photos along the edges, everyone could still walk around freely. The buildings along the street were thoughtfully designed as well. The books displayed in the Xinhua Bookstore's reading room were niche without being bizarre, numerous without feeling disorderly, and ornate without being gaudy. Someone was playing the piano, and the space was perfect for one person to calm down after the bustle outside and read without interruption. The books also suited Xi'an as a city. A bookstore really can be a city's soul. The Osmanthus Rice Ferment drink from Chahua Nong that night was genuinely delicious. When I had something similar from Chabaidao on October 30, the flavor was nowhere near as impressive. Chahua Nong emphasized the rice ferment and tea, while Chabaidao pursued the sweetness of osmanthus so single-mindedly that it lost the flower's clean fragrance. The Journey Home — October 29 We woke up a little late today and everyone slept comfortably. My body, however, had begun to react to the change of season, and my nose felt terrible. We only took a quick look at the Small Wild Goose Pagoda from the entrance because we were out of time, then continued to the airport. We did not talk much on the way. We were savoring this spontaneous, slightly fantastical journey as we boarded the plane back to Xiamen. It felt as though I had gained a little more sense of belonging to Xiamen. I still had more than two years left there, but I wondered when I would truly feel that I was also a part of the city.
